speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is reported that on June 1 the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) warned the UN Secretary-General, Javier Perez de Cuella, that Canada might withdraw its troops from the UN Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus. In so doing, the Secretary of State for External Affairs obviously reflected growing Canadian frustration at the apparent inability of the Turkish and the Greek Governments to reach a peaceful and equitable solution to the Cypriot problem.
Therefore, in the interest of the two disputing parties, of the Canadian public, and of the Canadian Armed Forces themselves, I propose that the question be brought to the attention of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for further investigation and discussion, and that the same Committee be empowered to study Canada's more general role as peacekeeper.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR EXAMINATION OF HOSPITAL SYSTEM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is, in Canada, something basically sick about our medical and hospital system. There are, at one and the same time, medical facilities boarded up, medical personnel unemployed or underemployed, and people who need medical attention, particularly surgery, who are unable to obtain services or who are forced to wait for excessively long periods of time. It is not uncommon for Canadians to go to the U.S.A. for medical treatment because they are unable to obtain it here.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) reduces, or threatens to reduce, payments to the Provinces and then, for crass political purposes, condemns her provincial
counterparts when they take the only steps available to them to help defray costs.
It is time we made a serious examination of our medical and hospital system with a view to removing the distortions, inconveniences, and dangers which have become endemic within it.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO VICTIM OF AIR CANADA ACCIDENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last evening 23 people died while coming home on Flight 797 from Dallas to Toronto. Among them was Stan Rogers, who lived in and sang about all the different parts of this country of ours, who sang about the hopes and dreams, all the promise of our land. He always sang about his Canada, and the people who make it great, the farmers and fishermen, those in the industrial plants and on the northern frontier. Some of his words:
For the good times come and go, but at least there's rain
So this won't be barren ground when September rolls around.
So watch the fields behind the plow turn to straight dark rows,
Put another season's promise in the ground.
That was from "The Field Behind the Plow", for Saskatchewan grain farmers.
Some more is for workers, from "Working Joe"-for Dad:
Time was when a fella could just let time slip away,
No worries, car or telephone, just rent and food to pay . ..
But now there's just too much to do in any given day;
The car, the phone, the kiddies' shoes, too many bills to pay ...
Oh it's sure sweet to sit at home and let time slip away,
Through tomorrow I'll be scratching through another day.
I am sure all Hon. Members of the House extend their sincere condolences to the friends and relatives, the bereaved, of those who died so tragically yesterday.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF BENEFITS FOR ADOPTIVE PARENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on March 30 I rose in the House of Commons to protest the inequity of Section 30(1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act. That Section required that an applicant for maternity benefits prove her pregnancy. As a consequence, adoptive parents were effectively denied the receipt of maternity benefits.
Section 30(1) was profoundly inequitable. Clearly, the general need for maternal care of the adopted newborn is as great as that required for the biological newborn to whose parents we have provided maternity benefits for many years.
As we all know, the inequity of Section 30(1) was eliminated yesterday by the passage of Bill C-156, which will provide either of the adopting parents up to 15 weeks of maternity benefits provided that he or she had met usual criteria of 20 weeks' employment in the previous 12 months.
I was particularly pleased to see the introduction, and passage by unanimous consent, of Bill C-156. I was also pleased to note an editorial, in the Edmonton Journal, entitled "No Less a Parent". The editorial, which was supportive of the extension of maternity benefits to adoptive parents, stated:
Employment Minister Lloyd Axworthy should be commended for his proposal to extend maternity benefits to adoptive parents.
I agree with the Edmonton Journal, Madam Speaker.

subsubtopic: SPRUCE BUDWORM INFESTATION OF NEW BRUNSWICK FORESTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in Canada the ravages of insect disease and fire consume almost as much forest growth as the forest industry itself.
[DOT] (mo)
Forests in New Brunswick cover 88.4 per cent of the land area. Most of this forest land, 15 million acres, is productive and represents an area equal to the combined areas of Vermont, New Hampshire and Massachussetts. The forest industry is the largest in New Brunswick, representing one-third of the employment in the manufacturing sector and 40 per cent of its output.
Direct employment in the primary and secondary sectors of the forest products industry involves some 16,000 persons, with indirect employment accounting for between 15,000 to 20,000 persons. More important is the fact that, of all sectors of the provincial economy, the forest products sector is unique in that it plays an important economic role in virtually all regions of the Province, in both rural and urban economies.
Because of the spruce budworm infestation, in southern New Brunswick in the 70s there was a loss of between six million and ten million cords of softwood. This approaches an
eight-years' supply of wood for the principal consumer and employer in that area.
The House of Commons forestry committee has begun an investigation into budworm depredations in New Brunswick. I thank the Minister for this move to maintain the forest industry which is nearly 30 per cent of New Brunswick's GNP. We must recognize the fact that this must be addressed as a farm type operation, and we must reconcile the conflict of environment and forest interests. The federal Government should lead in such an effort.

subsubtopic: GRAIN HANDLERS' DISPUTE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR URGED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure you are aware that there is a possibility of a grain port shutdown on the West Coast. In particular, there is a possibility of a lockout. Nine days ago, on May 25, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) a question about the possibility of appointing a conciliation commissioner or a board to try to make sure there was no shutdown, because this is a very vital time for the shipment of grain for western Canadian farmers. We are coming to the end of a crop year. It is a very important time and we cannot afford to have any kind of a shutdown which will jeopardize the economy of western Canada. The grain trade last year, for example, gave Canada a $5 billion export crop, and this is very important for the economy as a whole.
It is very important that the Government across the way should not once again sacrifice western Canada, as it is trying to do with the Crow Bill which is before the House. If it is going to reject the suggestion of a conciliation commissioner or a conciliation board, it should look at some other ideas.
I would like to suggest to the Government that it look at the possibility to talking to both the grain handlers and the elevator companies about the feasibility of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall mediating a settlement in this particular dispute. I remind you, Madam Speaker, that Mr. Justice Emmett Hall has a good reputation. In the past he has frequently been a mediator and conciliator. He has been very successful, and 1 am sure he will be accepted by both Parties. I ask this because we cannot afford to have a shutdown of the grain export industry-

of Sociology living in my riding, but who teaches at the University of Waterloo, is concerned over a current audit of his income tax returns for the past ten years. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I appreciate the Minister's answer. I also understand why he cannot give too many details at this time. However, concerning the observer he mentioned, may I have some assurance from him, even at this early stage, that the responsible Canadian authorities, be it an observer or otherwise, will be involved in the investigation so that in time we here will know through our own responsible officials just exactly what happened, so that this type of thing will not take place again?

subtopic: ATTENDANCE OF CANADIAN OBSERVER AT INVESTIGATION IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
This is the case, Madam Speaker, but the law and the tradition dictate that the place where the accident takes place commands jurisdiction over the inquiry. So if an accident takes place in the United States involving a Canadian plane, it is the American investigatory organization that does the work. If an accident happened in Canada involving an American carrier, the situation would be reversed. This is the practice between the two countries.
Obviously our observer is there and will do his job and he will know as much as the Americans will on the subject of the causes of the accident. But the causes are unknown now. Reference was made to a fire in the washroom, but I am advised by experts not to jump to conclusions before the investigation takes place.

subsubtopic: NATO-DEPLOYMENT OF WEAPONS IN EUROPE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. For the last year and more the Government has argued that as a member of NATO it is incumbent upon us to participate in the development of NATO weaponry, namely, the Cruise missile. Yet this week at the NATO Defence Ministers' meeting in Brussels three European members, Greece, Spain, and Denmark, refused to endorse plans to deploy Cruise and Pershing II missiles in Europe later this year. They are not being viewed as second class members. Will the Government follow the lead of these countries and withdraw its support from this escalation of the arms race?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: NATO-DEPLOYMENT OF WEAPONS IN EUROPE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have not supported the escalation of the arms race. This past week at Williamsburg the Canadian Government did everything possible to take a stand that would reduce the arms race and bring about results in the negotiations in Geneva.
I assure my hon. friend that one of the principal objectives that we pursued at Williamsburg, I think with some success, was to stress the importance of making progress at Geneva in order to reduce or possibly eliminate the necessity of deployment of missiles in Europe.

subsubtopic: NATO-DEPLOYMENT OF WEAPONS IN EUROPE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: At the same time as the Minister tell us this, the Minister of National Defence is in Europe endorsing the deployment of Cruise and Pershing-Two missiles in Europe later this year.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):

Of course, the first point is that the United States still has to make a request to the Government of Canada to test the Cruise missile. When that request comes forward we can examine whether these events to which the Hon. Member refers has any bearing upon our decision. It seems to me that they do not have very much bearing.

Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Madam Speaker, 1 think I told the Hon. Member the last time we had an exchange of questions and answers that at no time have I used the expression free trade. I have not used it at Williamsburg. Further they agreed that, as the recovery proceeds, they would attempt to reduce the existing protectionism. That is a new element that has not been evident in previous commitments at the Summit.

speechtext:

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Communications. speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: DECISION NOT TO TELEVISE FILM ON UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps I can answer the Hon. Member's question in part. I do not think it is worth while engaging in speculation on management choices in the CBC. As far as the film is concerned, an arrangement was entered into with Mr. Allan King and the Mengen Institution. Mr. King is a well known documentary film maker who has conducted some of the most important and prize-winning documentaries made in this country over the past several years. The contract arrangement we have with him was not in any way to have any editorial control. As we have discussed in the House many times, there is a very serious and tragic plight that people who are unemployed go through. It was important for other Canadians who had the advantage of having a job to understand that.
The point of the film was to try to undertake both the research and the analysis so that other Canadians would understand that kind of condition. I hope that the kind of filming that was done-and I have not seen it so I do not know what it contains-but I know the objective was a worthwhile one-I hope it has some public distribution.

Madam Speaker, given that answer, my next question is addressed to the Minister of Communications. If the film was that valuable why will the public not be able to see it? They can only have it one way, Madam Speaker. Either it is a worth-while film commissioned by the Government of Canada with the people's money and should be seen, or some officials of the Government of Canada made a serious error of judgement in the way the film was commissioned and made. Which of those propositions does the Government admit to be true?

Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, when we are talking about programming, the decision about what type of program is going to be aired over the CBC is made by CBC management and no one else. It is up to CBC management to decide whether it wants to air the film and whether that film is appropriate for airing at a specific time. The bottom line is

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister, in the absence of the Prime Minister. One of the Prime Minister's interventions early at the Summit conference was that France and Britain should be prepared to negotiate concerning their independently controlled strategic nuclear forces as if those forces were part of NATO's intermediate range nuclear force. This representation had been made quite frequently in international circles before, but usually by Russia.
Could the Deputy Prime Minister indicate what purpose the Prime Minister had and what results were obtained by the Prime Minister, acting as Russia's advocate in this particular area where he seemed to be suggesting that Britain and France should throw away the only bargaining chip they have in this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: WILLIAMSBURG SUMMIT-BRITISH AND FRENCH NUCLEAR FORCES-CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to answer that question. I can certainly remove from the Hon. Member's mind, I trust, the mistaken impressions he has about the discussions at Williamsburg.
At no point did Canada press that the British and French nuclear forces should be put into the INF negotiations. That was not pressed by Canada, nor did we ask that these particular nuclear national strategic forces go into the INF negotiations. What we did suggest with respect to that particular aspect, or at least what we questioned, was whether the type of document we were attempting to put together ought to include specific references to various negotiating positions that had been adopted. This is one particular negotiating position that has been adopted and which Canada accepts. The question is whether this document was an appropriate place for the inclusion.
I think the Hon. Member is also mistaken when he states that this is a view on substance which is taken only by Russia. I could cite some rather important persons in the West who say, at a certain point, the British and French strategic deterrents ought to be included in some way in the negotiation, not in the INF, but, rather, in some future negotiation.

Madam Speaker, the following questions will be answered today: Nos. 4,820 and 4,870.
June 3, 1983

1.	Was the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development advised by way of a letter dated April 12, 1983 that, because of financial constraints, the Eskimo Dog Foundation was unable to continue its work of preservation and breeding the Canadian Eskimo dog which has attracted so much international interest over the past few years and that the Foundation plans to donate its stock of some 60 registered dogs to the government on May 31, 1983?
2.	What plans does the Government have for the dogs it will receive and will it continue the work initiated by the Foundation of preservation of this unique and endangered breed?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2.	The Eskimo Dog Research Foundation was privately sponsored and organized. Its objectives were to re-establish the Eskimo dog as a breed and to have it accepted for registration by the Canadian Kennel Club. A secondary objective was to return breeding stock to Inuit outpost camps. The Foundation has been successful in achieving these objectives. Although the Department funded a film produced by Inuk Films of Yellowknife to publicize the work of the Foundation, and to assist it in raising funds, it has not been successful in this nor in selling dogs in the South and there is no commercial market for them in the North.
While the Department has neither the funds nor the mandate to underwrite the Foundation's operations, the Government of the Northwest Territories has indicated that they are prepared to assist the Foundation to distribute the dogs to individual Inuit hunters who can be expected to make good use of them.

1.	Is a conference on closed-captioning planned for Ottawa in 1983 and, if so, what will be the participation, if any, of the Government?
2.	What is the status of the Telidon closed-captioning decoder?
3.	On what date will the decoder be available for sale and what will be its cost?
4.	Is the decoder available as the Government had anticipated and, if not, for what reason?

In so far
as the Department of Communications is concerned, the reply to the above question is as follows:
1. On May 10, 1983 Communications Minister Francis Fox announced that the federal Government will contribute $30,000 in funding to the Canadian Captioning Development Agency (CCDA) to help sponsor the first World Conference on Closed Captioning.
The CCDA will host the conference as a special World Communications Year project in Ottawa this November. Existing captioning agencies in the United States, Australia, Britain, France and Sweden and other potential captioners will be invited to attend the conference. A special effort will be
Supply
made to involve organizations in developing countries that are interested in captioning.
2.	The Telidon closed-captioning decoder (with dual mode (videotex/teletext) capability) is currently operational and available.
3.	Due to the need to incorporate the final North American Presentation Level Protocol Syntax (NAPLPS) standard changes, the cost of the decoder is $3,950. It is expected that when the item becomes a consumer item there will be significant price reductions. Recent sales have largely been to people and institutions at the forefront of investigation and experimentation of its use.
Later this year significant price reductions are expected with a further significant drop in prices in the summer of 1984.
4.	As noted above, the decoder is available as had been expected.

BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-TRANSPORT POLICY Mr. Pat Nowlan (Annapolis Valley-Hants) moved:
That this House rejects the Government's policies with respect to transportation, which have caused concern, chaos and confusion, as demonstrated by its loss of control over Crown corporations such as Air Canada, CN and Canadair and that the political preference, secrecy and negligence that it has shown in its dealings with such private concerns as Maislin, and condemns the Government for its failure to demonstrate fairness, accountability and leadership in its activity.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am glad to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has returned to the House. As he well knows, this is an Opposition day on which we are expressing very justified concern, as far as the Opposition is concerned, about transportation policies and the fact that no matter how well intentioned this very pleasant and plausible Minister is, he is trying to adopt certain policies, in too much haste, perhaps biting off more than the legislative system can digest, let alone the public accept. Through this indigestion in the legislative process and the public's concern, there is confusion, chaos and concern of the public with regard to the transportation industry across this country.

Supply
I am leading off for my Party in this debate. My colleagues will be detailing aspects of this concern, primarily involving the loss of control which the Government should be exercising over its agencies, particularly its Crown corporations. We will be discussing its loss of control over Crown transport companies. It insults every Canadian when it appoints its political friends, such as Bryce Mackasey and Jack Horner, to top jobs. Then it heaps some more insults upon Canadians when it refuses to say what these men are paid, and fudges around in effect in regard to how much they work during the week for which they are paid.
Then there is the trucking industry. The Government's discriminatory support for a mismanaged company has dislocated the whole industry in central Canada. There are other signs of the Government's rot and lack of direction concerning transport matters. Canadian National is under investigation for illegal trade practices, and Parliament's supervision of the company must be suspended while Cabinet dithers about preventing CN from taking over a debt-ridden shipping group. Another colleague will be discussing that in more detail.
Then, of course, there is Canadair. It is, speaking most conservatively, in deep financial trouble. The trouble at the root is lack of control of the Government over one of its primary Crown corporations.
Then, of course, we have Air Canada, Mr. Speaker, and particularly the Chairman of the Board, a part-time chairman, whatever that means, and no one in this Government seems to know what it means. He is apparently under some type of RCMP investigation. Also, a consultant at Air Canada makes a secret multimillion dollar kickback deal, which I will refer to later.
These are just some of the matters, Mr. Speaker, which cause the confusion, the chaos and the legitimate concern of Canadians from coast to coast. We can consider too the very human element in the Government itself, and the Minister who is primarily responsible for the use of Government planes, and the rules as to the use or abuse of those Government planes. It appears that when it is brought to public notice through the press or in this House that Government planes are used to fly Ministers across the country-which we understand, but which is in effect mixing business with pleasure-there is a convenient bending of the rules. I would like to ask the Minister how he can justify bending the rules for Ministers when they file their expense accounts, and not distinguishing between expense accounts for personal pleasure involving family and expense accounts involving Government business. Canadians have just completed the most complicated income tax return ever designed to confound man. That Canadian, be it a working person or a business person must distinguish between the

business and the pleasure aspects in asking for some redress of expenses. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is part of the dry rot and alienation of the public from the politician, when there is a special rule which governs us and Ministers and it is not the same rule which governs taxpayers. That is something that, while it may seem small in terms of the dollars involved, in terms of principle is not at all small. It has to be addressed and redressed. There have to be firm guidelines set down as to the use of Government planes for business or pleasure.
1 say this kindly to the Minister, because I believe he is trying to do a good job, that, frankly, I feel he is trying to do too much in too short an interval. That I believe is best shown when we look at the changes to the Crow after 80 years or 90 years in a Bill which was supposed to be, perhaps not rubber-stamped but forced through this House by way of closure after a couple of days' debate.
Then in the East we have the Maritime Freight Rates Act under which the Government unilaterally, without consultation with the four Atlantic Governments, in effect contracted for a consultant group to review the impact and the continued efficacy of the Maritime freight rates, how they help or hurt the Atlantic industry. That again was done without consultation. There has been some clarification of that and, hopefully, when the report comes in from the consultant group there will be some chance for public input. However, Mr. Speaker, that is the point I make about concern, chaos and confusion. When you have those two fundamental Bills, the large one of the Crow in the West which affects all of Canada, and the Maritime Freight Rates Act in the East, and unilaterally the Government tries to force change through the House without proper debate or proper public input, obviously, you are going to get a negative reaction. I could speak at length on the effect of the changes to the Crow in the West and the Maritime freight rates in the East. One could almost say those Bills are like the wings of the economy. Those Acts are there for a purpose, to help build the economy in those respective areas. Those two Acts were the wings which gave the lift-off to the economy, to help the economy grow, to help the regions grow. Then, for whatever reason, we are told it is time to change. We all know there is change necessary in both areas. I agree with the Minister that change is needed. However, change should not be forced through the House with the club of closure.
There are many other areas I could mention, Mr. Speaker, for instance, what is in the paper today about Quebecair and where it sits. Evidently, Quebec has turned down the latest proposal from negotiations between Air Canada-the Government of Canada-and Quebecair. There may be legitimate reasons why it has been turned down. However, this is another area which affects a very vital part of the country. It is a very vital airline of the country and it is literally up in the air because the negotiations have not produced any results.
I do not have to mention Nordair and the flip-flops in Government policy on Nordair when it was taken over and when it was to be sold off. There is a total absence of any public statement from this Minister on the total area of

domestic air policy, which again creates chaos and confusion, and it certainly creates concern among all those affected. In fact, Mr. Speaker, one could say in a most poetic way that this litany of concern, chaos and confusion becomes a lament for a responsible leadership and for accountability of the Crown and its agencies to this Parliament, which is the representative of the people.
Others of my colleagues, Mr. Speaker, will be developing some of these themes, involving Canadair, Maislin, CN and CP. I would like to turn to the specifics of Air Canada about which, as many Hon. Members know, I have asked questions. It is called an Air Canada matter, but perhaps it should be called "the Chairman of Air Canada affair". We have a situation of indefinite allegations against unknown people for an unknown length of time. It may be called "the affair about people who are trying to set up the Chairman of Air Canada". However, all of this has little relevance to what I want to say about the Air Canada matter.
In my opinion, there are two fundamental issues at stake here which we have bandied about in the House through pleasant words with the Minister and even more pleasant diversions from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). One is the matter of the fair administration of justice and the due process of law. There is not an Hon. Member who does not appreciate the significance of that. The second matter, which definitely comes within the prerogative of this House and of the Transport Committee, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, is the conduct of the office of the chairman of a Crown Corporation, and specifically with regard to Air Canada, the problem of a parttime chairman wheeling and dealing for his own personal gain. This matter first arose in the House, Mr. Speaker, on December 9, 1982. On December 20, after reports in the press, the Minister of Transport, in replying to a question in the House, said that he telephoned the Chairman of the Board of Air Canada to tell him about an RCMP inquiry. The Minister said that he had RCMP approval to make the call. He further said that he had someone telephone the President of Air Canada. Not surprisingly, a further question was asked immediately, and it was, "What had the Minister told the Chairman of Air Canada?" At this point, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Mac-Guigan) intervened and answered that he had talked with the Minister of Transport and that he, the Minister of Justice, had taken appropriate steps, and that he, the Minister of Justice, did not think it appropriate to give further details.
For many reasons, Mr. Speaker, this answer is not satisfactory. The history of Parliament has long been a struggle to ensure that the executive is responsible to Parliament and, therefore, ultimately, accountable to the people. The simple belief of a Minister that his course of action is appropriate has rarely been accepted by the courts as adequate justification. The courts have inquired usually to see whether there were in fact reasonable grounds for the conclusion to which the Minister of the Crown arrived. In the court of Parliament, of course, the elected Government carries the day. If it does not wish to require the Minister to give reasons for his belief and to justify it publicly, then of course the Minister does not have to do so. However, this does not mean that the fundamental principle of responsibility on this issue has been discharged.

The people of Canada, to whom we are all responsible, sooner or later will merely say that on this issue the Government does not want the reasons for its decision made public. Perhaps we could say, charitably, that the Government will reveal some day why the Minister of Justice thought it appropriate not to explain what the Minister of Transport said to the Chairman of Air Canada. Very probably, the Minister of Transport acted perfectly properly. Very probably he told the Chairman of Air Canada nothing which would compromise an RCMP investigation. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, perhaps without even realizing it, the Minister of Transport said something to the Chairman of Air Canada, or something was said in the phone call to the President of Air Canada, that compromises the investigation.
This leads to a more fundamental point. Should a Minister of the Crown ever knowingly communicate with a person who, there is good reason to believe, may be under criminal investigation? On May 26 the Minister of Transport appeared before the committee and he was much more forthcoming about the telephone call. He said that he had made the call to the Chairman and he asked the RCMP for approval. He also said he was alone when he made the call and that there was no recording and it lasted approximately five, six or seven minutes. He said that he possibly told the Chairman that other people, presumably besides the Chairman, were involved in the police inquiry. I suggest that this is a most serious matter, Madam Speaker even if it was inadvertence on the part of the Minister. I am not suggesting in the least that the Minister acted intentionally wrongly when he phoned the Chairman of Air Canada. But I think this House should seriously consider guidelines which would ensure that the possibility of the criminal justice system being compromised or short-circuited cannot occur with phone calls to people who may be under criminal investigation.
We do not know, of course, whether the Chairman of Air Canada was himself being investigated. We can certainly draw some inferences in view of things that have happened since, but here we have a Minister privy to details about the investigation talking to a man who may be under investigation. Even if the Chairman is not under investigation, might it not be that a friend of his is? We have the Minister admitting that he told the Chairman that other people were being investigated. The possibility that a criminal investigation may be short-circuited or appear to be short-circuited and the suspects warned is very serious, particularly so in a case like this where the Chairman is a political appointee.
The Montreal Gazette has reported that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) attended a party given in honour of the Chairman's appointment. It would be a political embarrassment for the Government if such a person were to be convicted of a criminal offence, or even charged. I ask, should there not then be clear guidelines about the way in which Ministers and other

June 3, 1983
Supply
political appointees can communicate with a person in this situation so that justice will not only be done but will appear to be done?
The Minister of Transport has said that the RCMP-and by this he seems to mean one or both of the officers with whom he discussed the case-said that he could telephone Mr. Amyot. But should decisions about the due administration of justice really be left to be decided by RCMP officers in these circumstances? The answer must clearly be no. This House needs to establish clear guidelines on how political figures privy to confidential information about police investigations may contact persons who may be under investigation. I suggest, Madam Speaker, at the very least, an impartial witness should be required to be present and a recording of some type made of the call. But I am not convinced that any oral contact should be made at all. As I said, there may be, by chance or inadvertence, a compromise of due process. This is a serious issue of the possibility of political interference with the fair administration of justice, and I think we definitely have to set some guidelines. I would think that in time this issue should be clarified and defined before either the Standing Committee on Transport or a larger committee of this House.
Turning to the matter of conduct in office, regardless of what the criminal investigation is about, there is the issue of the Government's responsibility to ensure that the Board of Directors of Air Canada can operate properly, I have repeatedly asked the Government to consider giving the Chairman a leave of absence or suspending him pending the outcome of the investigation. I want to emphasize again that I do not make the suggestion because I believe or have any knowledge at all that the Chairman is guilty of any criminal offence. I do not know. I suggest perhaps that no one in this House knows what the Chairman has done or not done that may involve criminal responsibility.
Why are you charging him, then?

It is a fundamental aspect of our system of justice that a man is presumed innocent until he is proven guilty. However, there is the question of whether the Chairman of Crown corporation with a public board can continue to operate properly and indefinitely when he, rightly or wrongly, is at the centre, apparently, of a criminal investigation. I have had reports that the Board of Directors of Air Canada finds this to be an intolerable situation. In questions in the House, Madam Speaker, I have used the analogy of what happens when a policeman is under investigation. It is routine that the policeman is suspended pending the outcome of the investigation. There is some similarity with this situation because both have elements of public trust and it has to be clear that the public trust is not abused. There is no presumption that the policeman had acted improperly, but when the investigation is completed and the policeman is cleared, then he is reinstated. The suspension is not made or a leave of absence given because there is a presumption of guilt. The policeman is suspended because he occupies a position of public trust and responsibility-
But their pay continues.

Their pay continues, as my friend, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), says. It is imperative that the public perceive that there is no possibility that the public trust is being abused. I suggest, Madam Speaker, that the Chairman of Air Canada is in a position of high trust and responsibility in one of the leading Crown corporations in the public domain.
This Government may say that to remove the Chairman now would be to imply guilt. If that is in fact true, the situation has arisen only because this Government failed to give the Chairman leave of absence when it should have done so. When the Minister had this confidential information about a pending criminal investigation before anyone else even heard about it, that was the time for ministerial responsibility to be exercised so that Air Canada did not become contaminated through the criminal investigation. It was then the time to do so, at the very beginning of the investigation, before it ever got on the floor of the House and into the newspapers of the land. Sadly, Madam Speaker, I suggest that in effect the Minister is now reaping the penalty for his failure to discharge the responsibility that was clearly his. If it was not clearly his duty, it was clearly the duty of the Prime Minister who has the ultimate responsibility for Government policy. In this case I think he is very directly involved in the appointment of his friend, the Chairman of Air Canada.
There is another way, Madam Speaker, of looking at the matter of the Chairman continuing in his position pending the outcome of the investigation. Essentially he is appointed by the Government acting on behalf of all the people of Canada. The people of Canada own this airline, even more so than PetroCan where we have had advertisements saying: "It is ours". Well, Air Canada is ours. It belongs to the people of Canada. The Chairman is ultimately accountable to the whole country. Each Canadian is a shareholder, so the Chairman has a duty to explain his actions. If he does not do so, it is not that we say he is guilty of a crime; we just say he should not continue in the absence of explanations as Chairman of a Crown corporation.
There are many questions I could pose today, if I had the time, not about criminality but about conduct in office. The questions are very vital. I do not think it has ever occurred in the history of Crown corporations that one could even pose these questions, none of which have been denied.
We have an inquiry, for heaven's sake.

What has the Chairman of Air Canada failed to explain? There is the matter of his alleged request to TAP, the Portugese airline, for three free tickets to Portugal for his friends. The Montreal Gazette reported on April 27 that an internal TAP memo said that Mr. Amyot said he would be "very instrumental" in getting landing rights for TAP in Toronto. Now, TAP has very carefully denied that Mr. Amyot was actually involved in its efforts to get landing rights in

Toronto, but they have never denied they were approached by Mr. Amyot.

If he cannot or will not give an explanation, then he should be removed from his position as Chairman. Again, I am not talking about any criminal offence. If we cannot get answers from the Chairman of the Board, he should no longer stay as Chairman pending completion of this matter. In the case of the alleged request to TAP Airlines, it is particularly important to receive answers from Mr. Amyot because, as has been reported in the Gazette, if TAP Airlines obtain landing rights in Toronto, then Air Canada's business between Montreal and Toronto will suffer. Again, the Chairman of Air Canada has also failed to explain what connection, if any, he has had with Mr. Bertrand Dufour, the man who was trying to arrange a loan of $500 million or $1 billion to Air Canada. The Gazette has reported that Mr. Dufour is an associate of Mr. Amyot and is now in Europe looking for funds to invest in a resort project in Portugal in which the Gazette states Mr. Amyot is involved. Did the Chairman of Air Canada have personal dealings with Mr. Dufour at the time the loan negotiations were taking place? Again, there is the possibility of a conflict of interest, and Mr. Amyot should discount it or be replaced in Air Canada. He has the capacity to make any public statement he wants.
There is also a matter which Mr. Amyot should explain. I should point out that, like all the other matters which I mentioned so far, it is an issue which has been raised in the press and not first by me in the House. Therefore, it is not as though

Members will be speaking of accountability and the lack of control of Crown corporations. I do not want to trespass too far. I will not trespass any further, but let me say only that, regardless of the pejorative comments of my friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Flis), about my questions, the fact of the matter is that we know we have privilege in the House so that matters in the public domain can be discussed without fear or apprehension of having to run into men-of-straw lawsuits.

I will conclude as I began, by saying that I have a great deal of respect for the Minister of Transport and for many of his officials. However, I really do believe that, for whatever reasons, he is biting off more than he can chew. We know that he was under tremendous pressure involving the Crow when he did a flip-flop, which he certainly thought would help but which actually aggravated the situation. He is trying to bite off more than he can digest. The legislative process, let alone the people of Canada, cannot accept it all in a short duration of time to really make up for a great deal of inactivity over a long period of time. After all, the present Government has been the Government in power for the majority of time, sad as that may be for the Canadian public.
Therefore, I hope that the debate will focus on other areas where there is chaos, confusion and concern so that the Minister will appreciate that from coast to coast, in many areas, there must be a tenderness, a moving ahead and respect for the concern of people so that there are not closures on Crow and there is not silence on questions about chairmen of Crown corporations. Others will speak of other Crown corporations. These are questions which must be answered. The longer they are left unanswered, the longer suspicions will be created. The smoke is there. We all know that when one tries to smother a flame, it bursts out in other places, and it is not a very healthy situation.
I think that at least the Minister or someone in the House on the Government side must make a statement very soon to clear the cloud which is around Air Canada, rather than the cloud around individuals which is infecting and affecting Air Canada.

I would like to ask a question. Speaking of clearing a cloud, would my hon. friend leave us with a message before he finishes his remarks? Will he tell us if his Party is generally favourable to more control by the executive of Crown corporations or more control by Parliament on Crown corporations?
No, by Parliament.

Would he tell us whether his Party is in favour of more autonomy for Crown corporations? Would he also tell us whether his Party is in favour of more privatization for Crown corporations, or is it in favour of all four?
The answer to that could be another whole speech, which I will hopefully make some day.
Well, your general view.

My very brief answer is that we can philosophize about Crown corporations and, certainly, there are many areas where my Party believes in privatization. However, the big thing which is fundamental to the process is accountability. That is the big thing. That is the reason we are all here. The Minister knows, as a former professor, how we originated in terms of the battle of the purse and how this Chamber is the Green Chamber, the medal behind the shadows of the castle. Therefore, it could compromise the King's purse and did not have to send women, soldiers, cattle and horses off to the wars. The people resented it and fought the battle of the purse. We know it is difficult, with the complexities of Government, the complexities of Crown corporations and the amount of control involved, but that does not lessen the desire and the need to try even harder to exercise some control.
I do say very specifically that when Crown corporations are treated as political, personal fiefdoms, it does not help accountability.

could not or would not take part or, if it took part, required public subsidy.
I want to move an amendment to the Opposition motion because I think the accountability principle must be extended also to the shareholders and customers of private corporations in transportation as well as the public ones. I will not take a back seat to anyone, being in support of having a publicly owned national airline, a publicly owned national railway and several other publicly owned transportation utilities. I am not under any illusion that they will be perfect. Any organization run by people will be imperfect.
I will not hesitate to criticize any details of their operations or how they conduct their affairs if I feel it is necessary. We are fortunate that Air Canada is a Crown corporation. It is something which all nations have, all except one country to the south of the 49th parallel. All nations have a national airline for a variety of reasons, not just ideological ones. We agree that there are problems with the expensive golden handshake for management people compared with employees when they are being laid off or are trying to obtain early retirements and voluntary separations.
I question whether or not this is the time to get into a $30 million new head office. I question the misuse of the resources of Air Canada, whether it is by a member of its executive or anyone else. It is not surprising that, because of government policy, within the commercial marketplace in which Air Canada and CN operate, they cannot and do not operate any differently from private corporations which are in the same marketplace. Canadian National has been jacking up rates on containers shipped by rail out of Halifax while at the same time investing in competing shipping lines. I find that strange. Canadian National has abandoned branch lines in dozens of communities. One would expect that of Canadian Pacific, but one has to question that action when it is taken by a publicly owned corporation.
If the accountability of corporations in the private sector is improved, I submit there would then be less commercial pressure on Crown corporations to behave in the same way as do private corporations. In other words, there would be less pressure on Crown corporations to behave irresponsibly. Most corporations in the private sector which are involved in transportation are substantially financed and subsidized by taxpayers. They always have been. If the private enterprise system is so great in the transportation sector-and one could mention other sectors but we are dealing with the transportation sector-why has the private sector been incapable of doing the job by itself? It has always had to have public subsidy and public financing, and therefore it seems to me that the private transportation sector loses the right to claim that its work is private property and that it is confidential, that it is not as accountable as a public corporation is in the same endeavour and that it can do whatever it pleases. That has been the history of the Canadian Pacific Limited since 1881.

It seems strange to me that a private railway company can sit at the public trough and get subsidies and financing and not be accountable. How much do the shareholders of Canadian Pacific Limited really find out at their annual meetings from its officers about the company's internal operations and the use of the company's resources. Mr. Speaker, if you were to buy one share in Canadian Pacific Limited or CP Enterprises Limited and were to go to the annual meeting, you would see how far you would get when you asked what was happening to your investment. You would get voted out of order so fast that it would make your head spin.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that not only Canadian National, Air Canada and other Crown corproations must be accountable to a public body such as an appropriate standing committee of the House of Commons, but, in the field of transportation, so should the private corporations be accountable. Because most of these corporations exist only because of public financing and public subsidy, they are answerable to the public and the public is entitled not only to answers but, if possible, to some kind of social and economic return on their investment.
Let us take Canadian railways as an example. Taxpayers paid 60 per cent of the total original cost to build the CPR. Do taxpayers have any share in it? Do taxpayers have any say in it? Since 1881, Ministers of Transport under the law should, in theory, have been able to control the railways. We all know that they could not and they did not. Eighty one per cent of the investment for Canadian Northern, a private enterprise operation, was put up by the taxpayers, and 65 per cent of the investment for the Grand Trunk Pacific was put up by the taxpayers. When those companies went belly-up and Canadian National was formed, the taxpayers paid a second time. All of the bond holders got their money back. The banks and the financiers got their money back. We have been paying them off. We have been paying them back their original investment with interest. Over $2 billion worth of those debts have been transferred to the books of the Government of Canada. Canadian National is no longer victimized by operating losses because of the interest charges on those old debts. Who has ever asked those private sector railway companies to account for their practices and to account for what was done with public funds that were obtained?

Mr. Speaker, as I said a few minutes ago, on Fridays I always feel a little reflective and philosophical, so I have been reflecting, ever since I saw a motion would be moved concerning Crown corporations which, as we all know, are a phenomenon that is particularly popular in Canada. I do not think Canada invented the Crown corporation, but I do think Canada must have more of them than any other country in the world. Perhaps we should ask ourselves why this system is so popular in our country and what are the basic concepts of the
system of Crown corporations in Canada. It seems to me that the weakness in the speech of the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) was that he failed to discuss the philosophy and the concepts on which the Crown corporation is based. I do not wish to seem arrogant, but if he had fleshed out his speech a little by saying exactly what a Crown corporation is supposed to be and that the Minister of Transport was not acting in accordance with the principles of this system, I would have been impressed, but unfortunately I am not, because he failed to base his views on a more or less thorough analysis of the concept of a Crown corporation. In fact, that is why I asked him whether my hon. friend would like more control by the Executive over Crown corporations or more control by Parliament, and whether he wanted more autonomy for Crown corporations or whether he was in favour of privatization. I think all this is important. I have thought about it, and I know what I want. I am a Crown corporation enthusiast. It is one of Canada's great achievements. I think Crown corporations are respectable and I think we should appreciate the originality and the intrinsic value of this kind of system. I shall get back to this later on.
So what is a Crown corporation? Well, they are public enterprises whose shares are held by the Government. They have an economic purpose, at least the ones we are discussing today. Crown corporations in the transportation field have an economic function and purpose. They are created and governed by an Act of Parliament, by either specific or general legislation-in any case, I do not have to go into all that, since all this is generally known and they are accountable to Parliament through a Minister of the Crown, and it is a very essential characteristic of Crown corporations that they are accountable to Parliament through a Minister.
So here we have the whole problem of instruments, the entire range, if you prefer, of customary controls, which include the control exercised by the Minister himself, by the Executive, by Cabinet, by the Minister of Finance, by the President of the Treasury Board, and also by Parliament, which does so through the usual mechanisms of questions, debate, tabling of annual reports, and so forth, and last but not least, budgetary controls. So you see we are not particularly lacking in controls over Crown corporations. There may be a feeling that these controls should be improved, but the fact remains that there is a full-grown system in place with audits and what not. It is a complete system, created by Canadians, and it stands by itself.
In a few minutes, my Parliamentary Secretary, the Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis), is going to speak, and he will show how these controls have been improved in recent years and how they will be further improved in the future. The Hon. Member will talk about the progress that has been made in this area. I think we shall learn some interesting facts, such as the creation of a Crown corporation unit in the Department of Transport, whose task is to co-ordinate information. I do think we shall be hearing some very important and very

interesting facts. Mr. Speaker, this is not to say that we have no problems. We do have problems every single day, and they are brought up in the House in the questions I am asked. We do have problems, but I do not think we have a problem, that is, I do not think we have a really serious problem that threatens the very existence of Crown corporations. I do not think that is the case.
So what is a Crown corporation? I have tried to define this concept, but what is essential to a Crown corporation? It is a public enterprise existing within the framework of a mixed economy. In other words, we have Crown corporations or enterprises that are active in areas where the private sector operates as well. There is a measure of competition between the two. What is important as well about the Crown corporation concept is the fact that a Crown corporation is a public enterprise but nevertheless closely modelled after the methods, concepts, habits and techniques of the private sector. I want to emphasize this, because I think it is very important, and I am not being particularly original in saying that, because it is a commonplace in Canada. The Air Canada Act, for instance, clearly provides in Section 7 that:
"(2) In discharging its responsibilities under this Act, the Board-
-the Board of Directors-
__shall have due regard to sound business principles, and in particular the
contemplation of profit."
This is very important! Crown corporations are, in fact, hybrid institutions in which the private enterprise or rather the private enterprise philosophy has a role to play. Once again, all this can be found in any number of documents I could name, and I have an example here, a quote from Van Loon & Wittington:

-combining the need for some degree of public accountability with the freedom of initiative usually associated with private enterprise.
That is the conventional approach to Crown corporations, as I have been saying all along.

And that is what constitutes the value of this kind of enterprise and also its originality. Unfortunately, it is also the reason why Crown corporations are so often attacked. But why? Some people will say that it is because they are modelled too closely on private enterprise, and others that the resemblance is not close enough. And so the debate goes on, because some people, including the Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, are not quite sure about what they want. I do know what I want. I want the Crown corporation to have the goals of the public sector and the methods, techniques and psychology of the private sector.
I know what I want, and I think that as a rule, I do not contradict myself very often, because every time Hon. Members rise in the House to ask: "Does the Minister intend to tell the board of directors of Air Canada or CN or Northern
Supply
Transportation what to do?"-my answer is no! My answer is that I rely on the boards of directors of these corporations for handling routine business. In other words, I try to be consistent. I am not in favour of out-and-out interventionism on one day, and non-interventionism in the extreme the next.
One may ask why the Crown corporation is such a popular and widespread institution in Canada. If we look at the literature, it will give you five or six reasons to explain the popularity of this phenomenon in Canada. Geography and the demands of Canadian unity have contributed enormously to the creation of Air Canada and CN, for instance. There is no doubt at all that if this country were not as big and as sparsely populated as it is in certain areas, there would have been no need for the public sector to create these enterprises. The fact that we do have them is due to geography and politics. History, the Depression and the Second World War . . . During the Second World War, C. D. Howe, who was a private sector man if there ever was one, created 30 or so of these public enterprises. Another factor has been the increasing role of the State. The need to take up the slack of the public and private sectors has also been a factor. And in some cases, it was simply a matter of economic circumstances. I do not think we should make the mistake of assuming that the Government of Canada took over Canadair and de Havilland because of its socialist philosophy or just for fun or to be different. It did so because it had to. We had no choice. If we wanted to maintain this advanced technology industry in Canada, we had to act, and the Government's action was to create Crown corporations.
I am saying all this so that those who are listening will realize that the Government of Canada had a very practical purpose and very specific objectives in mind when it started creating these institutions. We must also remember that the popularity of Crown corporations is not restricted to the federal level but has filtered down to the provincial and municipal levels as well. Another important point I would like to make is that not one party in Canada has had a monopoly on creating Crown corporations. Many were created by the Progressive Conservatives, while the Liberals and Socialists have established a number as well.
My point is that although we may have reason to criticize the administration, operations and behaviour of Crown corporations, the fact remains that they respond to a basic given and need and to working methods that exist in Canada. Although criticism may be justified, I feel that as a general rule, we have every reason to be proud of what we have accomplished in this area in Canada. Once again, it is not something that is typically federal or municipal, Progressive Conservative or Liberal. In fact, what we have here is something that is truly a fundamental part of our political and economic life in Canada.
What does worry me a little, since this is an area where balance is of the essence, is that quite often I have noticed that some of my colleagues, and I am sure they are very well-

I was desperately trying not to see you, Mr. Speaker.
Oh, oh!

I was speaking of the general quality of these Crown corporations. Air Canada, for example, is the tenth largest airline in the world. It is considered by everyone, even today, notwithstanding the accident that happened yesterday, to be a very efficient airline.
The best.

Yes. Since recapitalization in 1970, its profits have totalled more than $200 million. It paid $53 million in dividends to the Government of Canada.
The Act states that Crown corporations should behave in contemplation of profit. They do maintain a high degree of efficiency. I was speaking of the awards they have received in recent days. In 1982, Air Canada received the Air Transportation World Award for technical management and excellence. Just a few days ago, it received the Design Management Award. In 1982, it received the Excellence in Communication Leadership Award. That is not bad, internationally. It has a very high reputation.
Advertising.

Yes. More recently, Air Canada was rated ahead of all trans-Atlantic airlines in passenger service by a prominent British travel magazine. Similarly, it has been avant-garde in service to handicapped people, for example. Similarly, it has one of the most sophisticated computer communication systems. This is a company of which I think all Canadians should be proud.
I respectfully submit that this applies to CN, too. CN has a great reputation for efficiency. I was in India some months ago and saw CN and CP jointly looking for a contract for the computerization of the Indian railway system.

But they will not fix their own tracks here.
June 3, 1983

Nevertheless, they have a fine reputation. Perhaps it is not up to the standard of the Hon. Member who would probably like to see the rails table flat from coast to coast.
Since recapitalization, CN has shown a profit each year, except in 1982 due to the economic situation. CN also pays a dividend of 20 per cent of its earnings to the Government of Canada. Since 1977, these dividends have amounted to $145 million. My hon. friend does not believe in profit and that kind of incentive.
I did not say that.

Well, we suspected that from what he said a moment ago when he appeared to be saying that he would like not only to establish a greater domination by Government and Parliament on Crown corporations but also to take over a number of other companies like Eastern Provincial Airways. He also mentioned Power Corporation and presumably he had Voyageur in mind.
Accountability with what they do with public funds.

Be that as it may, CN is consistently ranked among the top five railways in North America for its safety record. CN does 88 per cent of its purchasing from Canadian sources, which is a very high percentage. I could go on.
My hon. friend is correct in seeing some aspects of the operation of these Crown corporations and their relationship with the Government as worthy of his chastisement and occasional angry chastisement. I want to balance the facts by saying that this is an institution to which Canadians have contributed tremendously in its development. We see here a balancing act between the spirit of free entreprise and public objectives and necessity. We have companies that have operated in a mixed economy and I think this has been a balancing act that we can be proud of.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have one comment to make to the Minister. I listened very carefully to his position with respect to what Parliamentarians are about when they question the House of Commons, in the committee or when they assert, as I now assert, that Canadair is in violation of the Financial Administration Act. His position was that we are in some way attempting to control Crown corporations. That is not the purpose of those questions in the House and is not the purpose of questions in committee. It is not the purpose of our estimates process through which we can question Ministers and others.
What the Minister sometimes forgets and ought never to forget is that Parliament has no business as managers of Crown corporations. I know of no responsible Parliamentarian who would ever advocate that. Whether the Minister, the bureaucrats or the Government like it or not, our job is to hold Crown corporations or agencies accountable to the extent that we can with the machinery we have.
Supply
I want to make that clear because, in his George Bernard Shaw fashion, I believe the Minister was overstating the position that Parliament takes when it questions, doubts or raises alarm about occurrences in Crown agencies. I want the Minister to understand, and more importantly I want the public to understand, that as the Minister has the right to assert the place of a Crown corporation in the mixed economy or elsewhere, Parliament has a right to assert that those Crown agencies are under our control for the purposes of accountability. In many ways it is in our estimates that we grant a part of their funds and they cannot be separated. We do not want to run them; we want to make sure they are run properly.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased and honoured that the Hon. Member paid so much attention to what I said. If he wants to recall what I said, I talked about strikes, acquisition, lay-offs and about change in facilities. 1 was attempting to attract attention to the fact that there are more important matters to control. My view is a provocative reflection since this is Friday afternoon.
My hon. friend gave a speech of the same nature a couple of weeks ago. It is a thought that I have as a recipient of these questions and inquiries from Members who are looking for jobs for their electors and while it is all very nice, I must wonder nevertheless if we are not detailing our attempt to control these Crown corporations too much and should rather preserve our energy and time for the larger issues.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister very proudly announced the fact that Canadian National has paid $145 million in dividends since 1977. I believe that was the Figure and I presume it is the collective amount of dividends since 1977. He announced as well that Air Canada had paid $53 million in dividends. I believe this is a trend in the right direction.
Does the Minister have any figures on total dividends returned to the Consolidated Revenue Fund by our Crown corporations? Are they paying a fair part of the corporate tax load in Canada toward the provision of all the social services that we are so proud of in this country? Does he see any improvement to this? He has mentioned two Crown corporations, but are there others paying dividends and are they likely to pick up their fair share of the tax load?

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I am not an expert on the subject. I only have these two examples simply because I had them researched. My first reaction is that I do not think these cases of profit making can be generalized. I think that these are special instances.
I am enough of a socially oriented person not to be too greatly impressed by the size of the profit. I would have been more impressive had I been giving the size of the investments of these Crown corporations at the same time. The profit is nice but the extent of the investments that they make on an annual basis is a fact that I should have related as well.
It is my impression that CN and Air Canada are doing very well. They justify the pride we have in them.
