Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with the Minister's responsibility for transportation as it relates to the resolution, which states that it has caused concern, chaos and confusion. I would like briefly to outline a situation of which the Minister is very well aware and which I think can generally be applied to many other areas in this country. It concerns the community of Bella Bella which is suffering from very high costs, problems with the delivery of mail and problems with economic development. It seems that other federal departments are expending large amounts of money in sustaining a community through band administration, income support and economic development, yet the Department of Transport has failed to make appropriate investments to support those other Government investments. Therefore it is not only jeopardizing the community but the money that the taxpayers have put into there as well.
The Minister is well aware that the community needs a rollon, roll-off ferry terminal and requires assistance to complete their airport and extend the runway. Could he explain why the federal Department of Transport is not prepared to act in such a way that it will support the investments made by other federal Government departments? Why is the Department of Transport not ready to go forward and support a constitutional requirement? The Canadian Government has a constitutional responsibility to the native people of this country.
Mr. Speaker, one thing is clear: the question has nothing to do with the motion and nothing to do with what I said.
Chaos.

Yes. You can put almost anything under chaos. The answer to the question-I have not looked at it in recent hours or days, but I was aware of the speech my hon. friend made some days ago-is simply that there are two candidates for further airport development in the area. Nobody has been able to make a decision as to where the development should be. One thing is sure: the distance between the two sites does not justify the expenditure of millions of dollars on both. Possibly cowardly, we have left the decision to the Government of the Province to make, it being a more local question, and provincial Governments being more locally oriented. Apparently the provincial Government is not making the decision. My hon. friend is giving me good advice and I have been thinking about it. The time may come one day when somebody will have to stick his neck out.

Mr. Speaker, I have one quick question for the Minister. I notice that my good friend and colleague from Laprairie has been talking about the airline industry in the past and especially the position of the Crown Corporation, Air Canada, in that airline industry. Has the Minister given any additional thought to the possibility that there could be some further deregulation of the airline industry and a reduction of Air Canada's monopoly position within it?

Mr. Speaker, I have expressed my views on the subject during the hearings of the Standing Committee on Transport following a draft paper that I presented and following also an excellent report on the part of the committee. I could not agree with the committee on the role given particularly to regional carriers. I thought it was too fluid, too flexible. I was looking for something more categorized and I told them so very simply.
Since then my hon. friend, who is an ardent student of Canadian air matters, must have noticed some changes taking place. One of them, and I think this is very healthy, is the greater co-operation between airlines. Air Canada, for example, at the moment is working toward the restructuring of Quebecair. The Hon. Member has noticed also some kind of integration taking place between Eastern Provincial Airways and CPA. Again, these seem to me to be very healthy developments. A constant debate in Canada is: Do we have too many airlines? I would tend to believe that, although I will not be looking for a Russian approach to Canadian aviation-an Aeroflot approach. When I see these integration efforts I am very, very pleased.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very thoughtfully to the earlier remarks made by the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) and the response this afternoon of the Minister in a philosophical way about Crown corporations and what they are. The Minister in his treatment quite rightly said that we must be careful about choosing the points of entry with respect to influence or control over those Crown corporations.
Would the Minister not feel that one of those very obvious points of entry with respect to accountability must come about when there are two or three serious conditions precedent or apparent? One of those, for example, is an abuse of corporate office. The second is the apparent inability to operate within simple guidelines, Canadair being one of those in that particular case. Would the Minister not agree that those areas that are publicly discernible as meriting intervention with respect to accountability of Crown corporations should, in fact, be used by the Minister and be seen by Government as a responsibility to intervene? Would the Minister comment for a moment on the means of entry? He has told us that we cannot intervene on all subjects. Would he now talk for just a moment about how we identify the justifiable intervention processes?
Mr. Speaker, I would gladly allow the Hon. Member to keep on for another minute or two to illustrate in a more concrete fashion what he has in mind.

Mr. Speaker, I might very briefly. The difficulty with Canadian National Railways' investment in Cast has aroused the concern of the Province, of the principal marine community involved. Canadian National has without an objection from Government. If Government in this case chose not to intervene because there was no objection from the Canadian Transport Commission, I assume that is a reason not to intervene. But when that Crown Corporation-in fact, CN has had to write down $62 million-is contemplating a massive
June 3, 1983

further expenditure to acquire all of the assets, or the remaining assets in this case of the Cast shipping group, would the Minister not feel that in terms of accountability there should be produced for review by the standing committee or this Chamber, at the very least, the audited statements of the company to be acquired? I am throwing out these suggestions to see whether or not these are tangible, acceptable levels of entry with respect to accountability.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, there was hardly anything philosophical in what I said this afternoon.
That is right.

I somehow react negatively when I am told that what I say is of a philosophical nature. What I talked about this afternoon was a very practical, down to earth, everyday decision-making process, the pains and the flagellations of every day. Therefore, there is nothing philosophical.
Professorial.
The approach might have been philosophical but the subject matter was very concrete.
Very real.

Very real indeed. I am paid to know it.
On the subject brought forward by the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), I agree with him 110 per cent that the subject he has raised in recent months in committees and in the House is a very important one. I respect him and I admire him for the intensity with which he has raised it. There is no doubt in his mind and in the minds of many people in his area of Halifax that the takeover of Cast by CN, on which the Government has not yet decided, is perceived as having a negative effect.
I think he will agree with me that I have tried, possibly in an adequate way, to address this issue with him. I have talked with him. He has questioned me, he was nice enough to do so, on the importance of vertical integration. I have described the situation in the Montreal area to him with CP having a set of alliances with Manchester, with Dart, with terminals in Montreal, in Europe and in England, with all kinds of shipping facilities.
Having taken the position in the Montreal area that CN must react, CN cannot simply for the sake of being accused by the population of Halifax of doing something perceived as negative ignore that situation and let pass the opportunity of an merger with Cast.
I then tried to give the Hon. Member some information. This is all on top of what the CTC said in 1975. 1 tried to give the Member information on rates charged by CN. I tried to remind him also that CN has ownership in the area of Halifax. 1 tried to reason with him on the subject of cost recovery. I have tried to give him some information on the extent of the investment of the Government of Canada in the Port of Halifax. This is a very important issue. If one wants an idea of what I had in mind a few moments ago when 1 talked about
Supply
being selective in our debates on Crown corporations, I think this is a good example. It is a very important one.
Every day Hon. Members ask me why CN has laid off two people in X, Y or Z, or why CN has not bought a Canadian product in this particular instance. They ask me how come, et cetera. I think we should reserve our debates for important subjects such as this one.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister was very clever. He used up about 40 per cent of our total speaking time by eroding our objections. The old saying "He protesteth too much" is very apt.
The Minister was very selective of Crown corporations for which he is responsible. He picked out CN and Air Canada. He did not mention the losses of VIA Rail. He did not mention the loss occasioned by Mirabel airport. He did not mention the cost of carrying the Pickering airport land. He was very selective.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) gave a much better description of Crown corporations. They were established in the first place because they were in areas in which the private sector could not or would not take part and, if it took part, required public subsidy. It has gone beyond that. Also he mentioned the great C. D. Howe. Mr. Howe created a number of corporations in a wartime era. It was a necessity to survive World War II.
I am sorry the Minister has left the Chamber because I want to talk about his Department. When we ask him questions in the House of Commons, he always says that we should have given him notice. This indicates that his Department is so big he cannot control it. I would like to indicate for the record that the Minister does not know what is going on in his Department. He appointed Mr. McLeish as a consultant. He was the former deputy minister in charge of air transport. He was given the job of implementing the recommendations contained in the Dubin Report. The author of that report would not believe that the one man who was totally critical of him and working against him was the person who implemented the report because he did not believe in it. This proves that the Minister does not have control.
He talked about Crown corporations being in competition with the private sector. I could give a perfect example of competition between Crown corporations and the private sector. Petro-Canada receives money for every litre of gasoline sold across Canada. The money is used to acquire foreign companies which compete with Canadian companies. Canadian companies have to go into the equity and debt markets to raise money at high prices, so there is no competition. With the assistance that Petro-Canada has had, it still will not survive because it is in the marketing side as opposed to the exploratory side. I have to be brief in my comments this afternoon because I have to catch an airplane.

The Minister has left.

June 3, 1983
Supply

They are in Hansard anyway. My remarks will be recorded there and I can send them to my constituents.
It was interesting that the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) was here, waiting for what the Minister had to say. He has a problem of his own. He and a group of people sitting in that corner are on the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. They are having a hard time over the Canadair situation. In November, 1982, the officials of Canadair appeared before the parliamentary committee and did not tell the truth. They have been featherbedding the situation in Canadair for the last four years.
The entire story was told by "The Fifth Estate". I am surprised the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) did not kill that program before it hit the air. The present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) and former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce came out with a very interesting statement. He said:
1 was very lucky that I had just left the Treasury Board at that time, and I was just coming in Industry, Trade and Commerce, so the new President of the Treasury Board was not too much aware of what I was doing.
That is how it was funded. He did it on his own. It was probably one of the worst decisions the Government has taken in the last 15 years. It is just another example. It bought a company for $38 million some seven years ago. Last year the Government had to pump in $1,350,000,000, and this year another $260 million or $240 million has been requested. I get confused with all these amounts of money. The amount of money we have put into Canadair is more than the United States Government and the Canadian Government contributed to support Chrysler Corporation when it was in financial trouble. There are 4,800 jobs in Canadair. There are 150,000 jobs related to the Chrysler situation. That was money ill spent.
Now the company is blaming the engines. Officials say that what caused the trouble was that the engines were not big enough. That was stated by Mr. Bill Lear who designed the aircraft. He disowned it after it was redesigned by the people at Canadair. It was made big and fat and could not follow its original specifications. I am sure he would take back his original statement that there was no one in the United States intelligent enough to take this plane on. Unfortunately Mr. Lear is no longer with us. 1 am sure he would be disillusioned and would figure that if it were taken on as Canadair took it on, it would be a failure.
An example of what Canadair did can be found in the deal with Federal Express. Federal Express placed contracts for 25 airplanes. By the time the whole thing was over-and it only put down a deposit on one aircraft-Canadair paid $4 million to get out of the contracts and gave a plane for free. How can a corporation make money by doing that? It was ludicrous. It is typical of all Crown corporations in which the Government has become involved.
A Senator in Alaska was convicted for being bribed by Canadair officials to buy an airplane for the State of Alaska. Its employment record is deplorable. The Hon. Member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger) is somewhat disconcerted about the situation. He is more aware than anyone but no one will listen
to him. Canadair is not something unto itself. It is an example of the disrespect of the Government for the House of Commons.
The Auditor General should be able to review the operations of every Crown corporation. He should be able to check where the money went. If he finds that these companies cannot last on their own, they should be disbanded. We had a marvellous idea in 1979. We wanted to sell Crown corporations. Now they have gone so far down the tube that no one in the private sector would take them on. The only solution is to disband them, de Havilland is a prime example of Government corruption in the private sector. A friend of mine who was a very senior executive of De Havilland left that company when the Government took over. After six months, they had so much trouble that they asked him to come back. He only stayed eight months. In a conversation with him last fall, he told me that de Havilland was so badly run under the Government that it would never survive. The Government had destroyed all of the good that de Havilland had done. It destroyed any bit of credibility that de Havilland had built up. It ruined the company. It poured money into it, it had expenditures, it had people on the payroll. That is just another example of a very fine corporation that was destroyed by the Government. If we would have been able to stay in power in 1979, we would have put de Havilland back into the hands of the private sector and we would have saved a very fine Canadian organization.
There has been some talk that the cost of interest charges to Canadair equals 50 per cent of their sales. The truth of the matter is that that is not a representative statement because interest is not being charged. The Government knows that if interest is charged, it will just have to loan the money back to Canadair. There is really no interest being charged to Canadair at the present time on the Challenger mess.
Two years ago I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), who was then the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, if he would explain to me why all of the undercarriages that had been shipped down to Teterboro Airport, New Jersey, had to be returned. He said that he did not know anything about it. The truth of the matter was that they were replacement undercarriages that were too light for the redesigned plane. That is just one example that I brought to the attention of the Government two years ago, and if the Government had listened then, it would have known about the trouble it was getting itself into.
The Government has given us information about the tremendous sales that are expected for Canadair. Those sales have not materialized. As recently as last November, the Government stated that it would sell 142 planes in the next year. Mr. Speaker, only 76 planes have been sold since Canadair started in 1981. I do not see a very positive outlook for the future because Falcon and another company are far outstripping Canadair right now. Canadair's product is not the product it was originally advertised to be. It is a failure. It costs Canadair
June 3, 1983

twice as much to build an airplane as the purchaser pays for it. This is ludicrous.
We have requested that the Canadair officials who were here in November come back to the parliamentary committee. We hope that they will be back next week because those people did not tell the committee the truth. If I could use the appropriate word in the House of Commons I would, but I cannot. They told an untruth.
We now hear, Mr. Speaker, that this whole situation will be handled by Maurice Strong. We hear that Maurice Strong and Senator Austin will sort all this out. Well, I believe that it is now too late. Next week when Mr. Strong is before the committee, I think our recommendation to him will be to suggest that he winds up the company. There is no future for it. It will not sell products. Canada cannot afford to get involved in luxury airplanes. Canada can afford the work that de Havil-land did for many years. Canada can afford planes like the Beaver and the Dash-7 for short take-off and landing, but even these have been destroyed by the new Government management.
I will reserve my comments on that, Mr. Speaker, but I personally believe that the Government should not interfere in business. I believe that encouragement and tax incentives should be given to the private sector, and that if the private sector cannot succeed, it should be allowed to fail. I believe the private sector should be allowed to succeed in freedom and fail in freedom. I do not believe in putting a crutch under these companies as we did for Petro-Canada, VIA, CN for many years, and all the other corporations across the country.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member mentioned a friend who had worked at the de Havilland, had left and had then gone back again. He did not mention his name. I wonder if he would be prepared to tell us who it was who had all this talent and skill and could make these conclusions.

Mr. Speaker, as this gentleman is a very close friend of mine and held a very senior management position, I would not divulge his name in the House of Commons. If the Hon. Member wanted to check, I am sure he could figure out who I am speaking of.

Mr. Speaker, I would choose to make a comment on the position put forward by the Conservative Party. After listening to debate today and after listening to the Hon. Member's speech, it is interesting to note that we are talking about specifics of the transportation system that affect the lives of Canadians in small communities, and we have talked about native peole. We are very concerned that the position put forward by the Conservative Party today is absolutely devoid of constructive alternatives to the present policy. The Canadian people know that the Liberal Government is incompetent, and I think that in many cases they know that it has been devoid of principled operating decisions.
On the other side of the coin, Mr. Speaker, one of the most dishonest things that I have seen in my time in Parliament is

the current role that the Conservative Party plays by chastising and ripping apart the Liberal Government without putting forward a constructive alternative. There are many people in the country who need alternatives in order to make proper choices. I suspect that what we have before us is illustrated by what was said by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) in Maclean's magazine in May of 1981. He said: "Of course the Liberals are incompetent, but if I told you what our Party would do, the people would never elect it". I think that is the comment that must be made about the kinds of speeches that are being made today.
Just like its leadership candidates.

Mr. Speaker, I did say in my speech that I do not believe in Crown corporations. I do believe in encouraging the private sector through tax incentives. There are certain kinds of Crown corporations that were established by this Party and which had to be put in place because of the vastness of the country, but to put a Crown corporation in competition with the private sector is inequitable and unfair to the taxpayer because the taxpayer ends up subsidizing the Crown corporation rather than getting a deemed tax benefit from corporate taxes.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's last comment interested me. He said that he does not believe in Crown corporations. I think there are grounds for arguing in favour of more openness and fewer Crown corporations, but I would like to suggest to the Hon. Member that if the criteria that he suggested for determining the existence of Crown corporations were applied, that would mean that he and presumably his Party would privatize Air Canada, CN, Petro-Canada, and a great many other Crown corporations. Virtually every Crown corporation that I know of except perhaps AECL competes directly with the private sector in one way or another. If competition with the private sector is the criterion, is the Hon. Member saying that virtually all Crown corporations should therefore be privatized?

Mr. Speaker, I did say that there are certain Crown corporations that are required because of the vastness of the country, but 1 believe that any Crown corporation that can compete in the private sector should be sold to the private sector and that the Government should stay out of it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Debate. The Chair has been advised that the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) may have other obligations. It is not in the ordinary course of events that I should recognize him, but in the ordinary course of events I would look to the Hon. Member on my right. The Chair will need instructions.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has a long way to go. I would be quite happy to let him go ahead.

Mr. Speaker, today's debate is an important debate. I think it affords a good opportunity for Members of the House to comment on what could be considered the chaos, concern and dislocation that exists in the transportation system of Canada. In concert with

June 3, 1983
Supply
my previous remarks about the failure of the Conservative Party to express straightforward concerns that affect the lives of citizens of small Canadian communities, and because of its failure to express its policy positions on these vital issues, I would like to become very specific by choosing examples to illustrate where problems exist in our transportation system. The Minister and his Department must begin to act to bring transportation back to giving meaningul support to the economic and social life of Canada.
I should like to outline some problems that have been brought to me by people in the community of Port Hardy, British Columbia, regarding general aviation. People have questions about the dramatically escalating costs of the operations of General Aviation. They point out that the Minister and his Department have substantially increased landing fees at the airports, have increased parking fees and have created a situation where fuel costs for general aviation are exorbitant. The airport monopoly and, I would suggest, the price-fixing situation at many airports means that one litre of aviation gasoline in the area of 80 or 100 octane costs more than 60 cents per litre. That is absolutely absurd, Mr. Speaker. Basically it is unleaded pump gas. The cost is putting general aviation out of business.
The cost of radio licences went from $20 to $40, an unjustified 100 per cent increase which is passed on to the operators in general aviation.
The increase in regulations is a serious problem. We have no objections to safety and, indeed, commend the Minister on many of the things that have been brought forward to improve safety in aviation. We are getting to the point where we have regulation for the sake of regulation rather than for safety. This places more and more cost on the pilot and on the operator in general aviation. This point has been brought up by every operator I have come in contact with in my riding, every flying club, be it Sechelt at the Elphinstone Flying Club, the Powell River Flying Club, Comox Flying Club or at Port Hardy.
The other day the Minister bragged in the House that since he had imposed some of these cost increases he had increased the revenue from this source. I should like to tell him that from my examination of the situation at Port Hardy, it is my belief that he drove every private aircraft out of that airport. People flew into Port McNeill or somewhere else where they could store the aircraft and operate it at a reasonable cost. Some people just sold out because they could not afford to fly any more.
I should like to move on to other specific concerns of many Canadians. Within the air transportation system there is a group of dedicated, hard-working individuals-the flight service station air radio operators. Following the recommendations of Mr. Justice Dubin, the Minister recommended that these light service radio operators must control on and off runways, even though they operate remote stations. This was enforced. For example, a radio operator at one airport is
responsible, by a remote radio hook-up, for vehicle transportation at an airport at which he is not present. In airports such as Port Hardy, the radio operator cannot see all the runways on which he is required to control vehicles. I believe this creates a dangerous situation. We know it came about as a result of the Cranbrook air crash when a snowblower was on the runway at the time an aircraft attempted to land. I suggest that was not the fault of the radio operator but was a problem with airmanship, a problem with the plane, a problem with the communications system. But it was not a flight service problem. 1 suggest that Mr. Justice Dubin erred because sufficient information was not given to him.
The Department of Transport compounded the error by adding responsibilities for the radio operator which he could not reasonably fulfil. When radio operators reported that an error had been made, that they had inadvertently not given advice to the vehicle on the runway, the Department of Transport suspended some of them. The Department has been using tapes of communications in order to gather evidence against those people. I think the Department must remove the requirement that the flight service radio operator has to control traffic that he cannot see. That responsibility must be put back on the pilot and the vehicle operator who are the two people responsible, with assistance from the radio operator.
If the Department of Transport continues to suspend people who report operational problems and uses the tapes to reinforce that by gathering evidence, it is going to create a double-edged problem. People will not report operational deficiencies and that will jeopardize the safety of the system. This will also jeopardize the communications system because the radio operator will begin to be careful about what he puts on the tape.
I suggest the Department must eliminate the mandatory requirement for controlling vehicles by flight service radio operators. It must guarantee, through the collective agreement and through Department of Transport policy, that the tapes will never be used for disciplinary action but will simply be used, in co-operation with employees, to remove operational deficiencies. That is imperative in order to ensure the integrity of the air safety system.
I want to mention briefly the air accident which occurred in Cincinnati yesterday and to seek the co-operation of the Department of Transport to provide the information that I as a Member of Parliament want and which I am sure every other Member wants. I want the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to lay before the House information on the flammability of fuselage interiors in major commercial aircraft.
I want the Minister to provide information about the production of poisonous gases from the combustion of material in the aircraft fuselage.
I should like the Minister of Transport to also lay before the House an explanation of firefighting equipment, fire-detection equipment, training programs and safety procedures in major commercial aircraft terminals.
June 3, 1983

I should also like to know what is available in terms of personal fire protection equipment for passengers on major commercial airlines, and the adequacy of such equipment.
The tragedy in Cincinnati has created a situation that I know has concerned many people for a considerable period of time. It does not relate to the present accident. It reminds me and others of situations which have occurred in the past but have been left fallow. I believe the Department and the Minister made commitments to produce such material and it is time it was laid before the House.
I should like to move to another area of chaos in the system, Mr. Speaker. The Dubin Commission talked about the Air Accident Investigation Tribunal. That legislation was ready before Christmas; it has been delayed long enough. That Bill must be brought before the House before we adjourn in June so that we can look at it over the summer and be prepared to move on it in the fall.
I want to talk briefly about the community of Bella Bella and the Indian Heltsuk Band. The Indian name of that community is Waglisla. Millions of dollars are spent in that community by the federal Government on the 1,000 people who live there. It is provided through Band administration funds, unemployment insurance, economic development-it all hinges on a reasonable transportation system. The transportation system is not being used to support federal Government investment in that community. The transportation system and the Department of Transport, by their failure to act, are jeopardizing a great amount of taxpayers' money.
I should like the Minister to explain to the House how he can fail to fulfill the Government's constitutional responsibility to the Indian people. There are 1,000 people in that community whereas in the community he mentioned on the other island, which is half a mile away, where the Government is allowing the airport to be built, there are only 60 people. The hospital, the doctors and the places where medical evacuations will occur are all in the community on the Indian side. The basic thrust of economic development is on the Indian side. The taxpayers' investment is on the Indian side. There is a constitutional requirement to support Indian people and there is also a logic for doing so.
It just defies description that the Minister can avoid putting in that facility. That community has needed for years and years a roll-on, roll-off ferry. The ferry pulls in and out but there is no roll-on, roll-off facility. That simple fact has driven the cost of living up in that community beyond what any of us would ever tolerate, and it has also meant, because of the failure to develop an adequate transportation system, that the mail system is chaotic and that their economic development is bound for failure. It debilitates any attempt at constructive planning and development in that community. The Minister said it is a bit of cowardice that we have not made a decision on it. It is one of the most cowardly acts which I have seen in this House. It is an absolutely wrong-headed, counterproductive process which the Government is taking today. I would
Supply
urge the Government, if it does one thing before the people of Canada, in justifiable outrage, throws the Government out of this House, to please put in that facility. Do something which is morally and appropriately correct.
My constant theme when speaking about the transportation system has been Bella Bella, because it illustrates problems in coastel communities. However, that problem extends from Alaska to the 49th parallel in small communities up and down the coast of British Columbia. The Minister mentioned the provincial Government. The provincial Government has failed to fulfil its responsibilities to communities which are not native communities. So be it. That is a provincial responsibility and it has jurisdiction there. However, this Government has a responsibility to Indian people which they are failing to deliver.
For the edification of the Minister and the officials of the Department of Transport, I would like to point out that there is a community at Klemtu, the Kitasoo Band. Several hundred people live there and are struggling with air transportation, which is irregular and very expensive, and a mail system which is disrupted. They cannot function properly with Band administration and with economic development because of the failures in the transportation system. They could not get their kids home from boarding school one Christmas because the ferry does not go in and out of there on a regular basis. They need an appropriate facility and they need the federal Government to tell the Province of British Columbia: "If you accept federal assistance you must provide decent service to Indian communities"; or the federal Government must ensure that its responsibility is fulfilled. Klemtu is a perfect example.
Owikeno is another perfect example. Alert Bay is another. I would urge the Minister of Transport and this Government to take a very hard look at native communities from Alaska to the 49th parallel border with the United States, at how it is fulfilling its responsibility, and that its failure to fulfill its responsibility properly is jeopardizing millions of dollars which are being invested in economic development, income support systems, and Band administration in those communities. It is vitally important to remember, Mr. Speaker, that regardless of where we are today, and of where the provincial Government is today, the Canadian Government has a constitutional responsibility to support Indian people. The Government also has a rational responsibility to protect the investment of the taxpayers of Canada who want the programs to go ahead in that community.
I believe that the points I have raised on the air transportation side are extremely important. The Minister should be presenting that material to the House so that we know where we are going with it. The second issue is that responsibility to Indian communities is paramount. I hope that before we leave this Parliament there will be some action in an attempt to rectify long-standing wrongs in that particular area.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions, comments, answers? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate this after-

June 3, 1983
Supply
noon. I read with some interest and, I must say, some confusion, the motion of the Official Opposition. It is a typical Opposition motion in that it covers the whole waterfront; it covers the ball park, has everything in it that you could want, but yet has no particular focus.
I thought that possibly by listening to the address of the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) we might get some idea of just where the focus would come. I listened but I listened in vain. Something I did agree with in what the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants said was his compliment to our Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin).
In looking at the candidates for the Leader of the Official Opposition Party, I was thinking that one is bilingual, one has business experience and another has other attributes, having lived in Quebec. How fortunate they would be if they had our Minister of Transport as a candidate. He is fluently bilingual, a businessman, has had experience in the House of Commons and has the talent and ability to the extent that he receives compliments from Members of the Opposition Party. If they had one like him as a candidate for the leadership, it would be a shoe-in. We are proud of our Minister of Transport. We recognize that he also had the intelligence to pick the right Party of which to be a Member.
If one reads the motion, one sees the Official Opposition saying something like "losing control of Air Canada", and yet I wonder what is the position of the Official Opposition. We have leadership candidates telling us they would sell Air Canada which, of course, would mean no control of Air Canada. Are we to believe the leadership candidates, one day one of whom will be leading this particular caucus, or are we to accept what the caucus says, that we should have more control over Air Canada? I would be an interesting debate to take place, I am sure.
Everyone has their own particular gripe with Canadian National, Mr. Speaker, whether it is the fact that the freight is not picked up on time; but I believe the Minister hit the nail on the head when he said: "That is not the sort of thing we should be debating in the House of Commons. It should be the more important issues as they affect policy, the over-all position of Canadian National as to whether it should or should not be participating in a particular project."
One of the concerns I have is the recent move to some rationalizing, which is spreading fear among employees of Canadian National. These are people with 15 years and 20 years' experience, that kind of seniority, and they have some apprehension about their jobs because of the centralizing which is taking place, in the interests, of course, of saving money, perhaps, in the long run. I think it is those people we should be putting the emphasis on at Canadian National. People who have given CN 15 years and 20 years of their lives should not have apprehension about possibly losing their jobs because someone else has 25 years' experience, and seniority will out. I believe there is a social obligation which CN has and we should be focusing on that if we are looking in this particular area.
We have heard comments today about Canadair. I believe here again we have the destructive force of the Conservative Party at work. We are reminded of the Avro Arrow which was put out of service, in effect closed down by the Conservatives because they could not stand the heat of some problems which the Avro Arrow was facing at that time. In the long run, however, what a terrible cost to Canada! The technology which we had in place and which would have put Canada in the forefront of the air industry we lost because our technologists went to Houston and created great names for themselves in NASA. By its very nature the aircraft industry is the kind of industry which requires trial and error, requires the use of various components, in order to put the best mixture together and come out with the best aircraft. The same is true with the Challenger aircraft. To have it pilloried by the Opposition Party I believe does a disservice to the Canadian people who are endeavouring to make this work.
I was surprised to hear today the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) blithely say "Close it down, shut it down", because Canadair is having problems at the present time. That surely is not the approach, Mr. Speaker. Surely the approach is to do what we can to preserve this particular enterprise and make it a success. It was interesting to hear the Hon. Member for Ontario comparing figures about what the Government of the Province of Ontario and the federal Government have done with respect to loan guarantees for Chrysler, and how Chrysler is proving to be a marvellous success. All of a sudden that is a good idea. But it was not a good idea at the time as far as the Official Opposition was concerned. Fortunately, we did not panic and took the moves which were necessary in order to preserve the company, yes, but, more importantly, to preserve jobs, something which is important to Liberal Members of Parliament. I would hope they would also be important to Opposition Members. Now they seem to be applauding the actions we took at that particular time.
When I talk about Tory tactics of destruction, I think of questions asked by the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) where she selectively pulled something out of a particular report and said: "Well, the planes are useless during many weeks of forest fire season; the planes are supposed to get water but the water is covered with ice". She went on to say that because she was from British Columbia she had spent a good deal of time in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and knew this. What she neglected to mention is that that is not the height of the forest fire season in the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Like her, I have spent time not only visiting, as she apparently did, but I actually lived in that particular area for more than a year and know something about freeze-ups and breakups and times when fire hazards are at their peak. We know the peak is in July and August when the lakes are free of ice and when these particular water bombers can do the job they were designed to do. Neither did she make reference to the fact that they can be filled up with water on land or that chemical retardants can be used in the event it should be

June 3, 1983
necessary during the freeze-up period. The plane does not require open water for operation. Fully loaded, it can take off from hard-packed strips as short as 3,500 feet. So there are actually a greater number of airfields available to the water bomber than to the aircraft presently in use, which requires a 5,000-foot runway for its operation.
We are looking for international markets, Mr. Speaker, and to Canadair's credit they have found international markets. But bad mouthing and criticism of the sort we have had recently does not do a great deal to help us move into international markets.
On May 29, for example, Canadair signed a multimillion dollar contract with Lockheed-Georgia Company of Marietta, Georgia. This contract calls for the Canadian aerospace firm to provide components for the new Lockheed C-5B military air transport. The U.S. Air Force plans to buy 50 of these aircraft. Canadair will build the aft cargo doors, the ailerons, the leading wing edges and other components of the new plane. This is the kind of initiative we want to encourage because it means a $200 million contract and 700 Canadian jobs between now and 1986. If we close down Canadair, Mr. Speaker, not only would we not be participating in this kind of contract, but that money would not have been available to the Canadian economy.
As I indicated, Canadair manufactures the water bomber. It is a twin-engine amphibian used mainly to fight forest fires. Seventy-four have been sold to customers in eight countries, including France and Spain where it is widely used. The federal Government and six provincial Governments recently announced plans to assemble a fleet of firefighting planes using the CL-215. Here again is an excellent illustration of cooperation between the provincial and federal Governments. There is direction from the top, not a lack of direction as the Opposition motion seems to indicate.
Canadair has built more than 3,900 aircraft since 1944, 580 of which are supersonic. Canadair's project to develop the Challenger as a wide-body transcontinental business jet should be encouraged. Admittedly we have to look at any problems which may arise, but there are ways of being critical without putting it in the public eye to the point where people in the international markets look at this and say: "Well, we are not going to buy that; it looks like a turkey". That makes the task of Canadair all that much more difficult. So far 76 of these planes have been delivered.
The motion seems to suggest a lack of control, Mr. Speaker. But recognizing the problems in companies such as de Havil-land, Canadair and others, and recognizing there has to be some measure of business expertise brought to bear to help out these particular corporations, the Government announced the Canada Development Investment Corporation as a means by which this kind of business expertise can be brought to bear so that companies having difficulties will have access to this kind of assistance.
We know that Canadair and de Havilland are incurring significant losses. Of course, this is partly due to the international recession. A great deal of CDIC's time has been spent on financial and marketing analysis, particularly in the case of
Supply
Canadair. A short time ago the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) tabled his supplementary estimates which include provision of $300 million for the aircraft companies. This amount will ensure that these two companies continue to operate in the normal course of business while the process of analysis continues. The goal of CDIC is to put both of these companies on a basis which will allow them to continue to operate without substantial requirements for equity investment for their current products. The CDIC legislation stipulates that new programs and products would require new investment.
There have been some suggestions that this is being done on the quiet or that there is not enough information available. Well, the Minister responsible for the CDIC has advised the chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs that he would appear, along with officers of CDIC, before the Committee on June 7 to provide a report on financial and other business matters concerning Canadair and de Havilland. At the same time CDIC officers will appear before the Public Accounts Committee to discuss Canadair.
Members will agree that a start has been made in the right direction by CDIC to strengthen these aviation companies to ensure that Canada is an international competitor in this very important high-technology industry for many years to come. Surely that objective is more appropriate than simply throwing up your hands, as the Hon. Member for Ontario would do, and saying: "Just close Canadair down, it's a loser". Well, thank heaven that is not the Liberal Government's approach. I am sure the employees of Canadair will be interested in hearing the Hon. Member's comments. I hope he is not speaking for his Party, if anyone can in fact do that at the present time.
There are occasions, Mr. Speaker, when a key industrial enterprise requires Government help to help it overcome difficult times. If such companies have the capacity to recover, with some help, then it makes little sense to see them fail. Not only would the Hon. Member for Ontario see them fail; he would push them into failure.
No, Mr. Speaker, that is not the way we should be operating in this country, particularly when we are talking about difficult industrial enterprises such as the air transportation field. What the Government needs is a professional, experienced and commercially-oriented source of advice on how to handle specific situations in the future. Of course, not every company seeking help should get it. CDIC will operate in close contact with the business and financial community. It will, naturally, be a useful source of advice on business conditions. It will provide advice on where Government assistance might be beneficial or what financial alternatives are available in each situation.
Some two years ago, in an address I gave to the Sarnia Rotary Club, I indicated that we had to stop this ad hoc approach to helping industry, be it Dome, Chrysler, Maislin, Canadair, de Havilland or whatever. People come with best intentions and an obvious need for assistance and decisions have to be made by provincial and federal Governments almost

June 3, 1983
Supply
on an ad hoc basis. As a matter of fact, that is pretty well the way it has been done. Here we have the CDIC which will bring about a more professional business-oriented approach so that companies, if they seek help, will know what the ground rules are. The Government will also have some guidelines established so that it will know which companies it should help and those it cannot.
I welcome the pragmatic response by Government which I think CDIC provides to the needs of this particular day. It will help manage better what the Government already owns. It will provide important advice. It will be an extra means for Government to help rebuild our industrial sector at a time when Governments throughout the western world are taking strategic steps in key areas, such as aviation/aerospace, microelectronics and computers, and telecommunciations, to ensure they can participate in these vital industries of the future.
If I have a fault to find with this motion of the Opposition, and there are many faults to find, it is the fact that there is a lack of focus. I think that was borne out by the Hon. Member for Ontario because, when the Minister of Transport responded in a positive and, I thought, effective way to the questions which were being asked, the Hon. Member for Ontario immediately retreated to another ground and said; "Oh, yes, but you did not mention this and you did not mention so and so". It is not the motion of the Minister of transport that we are debating today; it is the motion of the Official Opposition. The Minister was confining himself to the subject matters raised in that particular motion. I think it was appropriate that he should do so, trying, at least, as best he could, to give some focus to the debate, which we have tried to do.
I think the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party who last spoke discussed many of the local situations and issues. However, in the final analysis, he was saying to the federal Government; "Direct the Province. You people have done something. You are making money available in British Columbia in these particular areas to do these particular things. Now tell the British Columbia Government that it must take some initiative and do the sorts of things that the federal Government is doing. It is putting money, expertise and help into these areas; but it does need some help from the provincial Government". So his chastising, if you will, was primarily directed at the provincial Government rather than at that which the federal Government has been doing.
Rather than losing control, I think the federal Government, through the creation of the CDIC, through the help which it has given to various industries rather than closing them down, through a whole series of actions, has shown that it is taking control in the areas where it should be moving and leaving to the private sector that which the private sector can do so well.
Mr. Speaker, it is Friday afternoon and here we are again-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: The House is full.

-with a full House and the Minister present, and I appreciate that very much, Mr. Minister. I have been quite interested in the nature of the Minister's remarks.
He gave us a little lecture. He said that a Crown corporation, with shares held by Government, must have an economic purpose governed by legislation and be accountable to Parliament through a Minister. As we have moved to a corporatist society, we have gone way beyond those definitions. If we are limiting ourselves strictly to some 57 Crown corporations under the legal definition, then that is one thing. If we are discussing the creation of non-governmental bodies with unbelievable powers outside the realm of surveillance, questioning and inquiry on the part of the House of Commons, then that is quite another.
What is happening is that a subgovernment outside of the purview and examination of parliamentary committees is running quite out of control. If it has an economic purpose, that is one thing. I am standing on this side of the House with a Party which has been responsible for the incorporation of many of our Crown corporations. Back in the history of that evolution there was such a need on the part of Government because infrastructure had to be built and the scales of economy and the marketplace just were not sufficient to cover the investment needed on the part of the private sector.
We seem to have gone through a series of phases in history in terms of Crown corporations. We have gone beyond the phase when we needed the CNR and when the Government had to help the CPR. Unlike the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and the NDP, I am glad that we have a private sector railroad and a government sector railroad. They keep each other in balance and they should keep each other from causing a monopoly to develop, because nothing in the way of infrastructure affects our lives more than transportation. One must only consider how the villages of the United Kingdom opened up when canals were dug to connect one group of tradesmen to another group of craftsmen. This competition led to the industrial revolution. That is the way it has been. We have gone through rail, through ships, slow ships and now high-speed ships, from bulk handling into container handling and unitized handling. It has been necessary for the CNR to go into fields where it has had to become involved with Cast.
I guess what is troubling so many of us in the House of Commons and people in the country at large concerns the question of accountability. Where is the accountability and the answerability? Who is impressing upon these non-departmental bodies, these Crown corporations and these Ministers to whom they are supposed to be answerable, how well the investment is being used?
We hear of the great need for a mix between the private sector and the Crown sector or Government sector. That is fine. What is so different is that the private sector is held accountable by the tax collector. The Income Tax Act states that one can do this and one cannot do that, and that one will pay taxes. If one has losses in the private sector, there is no way out. The bank and the debtors call one to account and one is out. However, those rules do not apply to the Government
June 3, 1983

sector, the Crown corporation sector and the Crown agency sector.
What we are doing here is giving these Government entities a special set of rules. We are giving them Her Majesty's agency status. We are incorporating them under Acts of Parliament and under the Canada Business Corporations Act, which is an entirely different ball game. They are exempt from the rules and laws of the Provinces. They can borrow money at the cost of the Government. They have Government guarantees and are exempt from the rules and laws of the land which apply in terms of competition, because in Government agencies, with agency status cartels are completely legal. One cannot touch a Crown corporation, or a Government body which has agency of Her Majesty status, that performs acts that would put any of the rest of us in jail or bring us before the courts.
What has been done? The Government has overbalanced, overloaded and tipped the whole pile of wood over in favour of non-accountability. Human nature being what it is, whether it is in the private sector or in the Government sector, bureaucracies being what they are, all that is involved is power. To me, there is very little difference between bureaucracy in the private sector vis-a-vis bureaucracy in the Government sector or bureaucracy in a large corporation. It is all power. The great untaxable thing that we are facing today is the privilege and enjoyment of power over people, over money, over decisions and over assets. The rule books are different.
Therefore I can tell Your Honour, and I hope the Minister is listening, that there is no way the private sector will survive unless we hold this subgovernment sector to account to the House of Commons through House of Commons committees. It is accountability, answerability and value for money concepts that are so important today. I cannot understand why the Government keeps resisting the need for stronger parliamentary committees which can deliver a high standard of accountability.
I will say to the Minister through Your Honour that in no way, shape or form does the Opposition or do the backbench Members of Parliament want to interfere with the Government's right to govern. In no way, shape or form is that the objective. In no way, shape or form is the objective for control to be in the House of Commons. However, if the system is to survive, and if there is to be competition which forces better ways of doing things to turn the nation into a more productive one, and to give us the drive and the environment to do things better and to achieve our place in world markets rather than through cartels and monopolies, then there will have to be some answerability and accountability through the House of Commons system.
I would plead with the Minister to support some of the action and very hard work being done by Members on all sides of the House in this direction. For instance, the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure has been working in this area for some nine months. If we do not bring about that condition of answerability and accountability and
Supply
we let the rule books and accountability standards remain so uneven, I can envisage the private sector disappearing altogether.
For example, we heard the Minister compliment Air Canada. If I was the Minister of Transport I would be very proud of Air Canada as a Crown Corporation. But may I say that some years ago, back in the Thirtieth Parliament, I was lobbied by Air Canada pilots who told me of the terrible conditions and bleak future of Air Canada if the top personnel was not changed. We were fortunate as a country to have Mr. Taylor come in as Chief Executive Officer. He knows how to run an airline and every other airline in the world knows it. He does a first-class job and, in my opinion, he is a first-class executive. But how can a competing private sector airline survive with the advantages that Air Canada has? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) just told us this afternoon that Air Canada has had to pay approximately $56 million in dividends. Last year, Air Canada was involved in a $38 million loss in its last quarter yet it was able to cut its tariffs and selling prices by a very substantial amount in the peak season.
To fill the planes.

To fill the planes. It was losing $38 million but was in a position to cut its tariffs in the peak season in order to fill the planes when the private sector airline could not do it. In that same period the private sector airline lost its working capital. If it were not the subsidiary of a corporation as large as Canadian Pacific investments, it would not exist.
I have been suggesting in the House for some time now that if we were not able to cancel the debts of Canadian Pacific Airlines in the same way we cancel Air Canada's debt-if the equations were not in balance-there would be no way for the private sector airline to compete with a Government subsidized airline.
I speak of CPA because their head offices are in my region. I want to see that payroll survive as, I am sure, the Minister does as well. The factors must be balanced. It is easy for us in the House to cancel the debt of Air Canada. It is the only airline in North America that need not worry about having so much equipment backed up against the fence. It is the only airline that can survive while having so much equipment unused.
On the other hand, CP has one of the best records in the world in terms of air time on their equipment. They must make full use of their equipment because they cannot survive unless they implement every single productivity trick in the book in terms of productivity. This involves the management of capital, capital equipment and personnel. The personnel at Canadian Pacific have a different spirit because they realize the delicacy of their jobs.
I will say again to a very reasonable Minister of Transport-[DOT] as long as he does not bring in the Crow-that if this equation is not addressed I must come to the conclusion that it is a deliberate Government policy to peel the orange of Canadian Pacific Airlines with all that will do.

June 3, 1983
Supply
I can suggest what the Chief Executive Officer of Air Canada will do if the orange of Canadian Pacific Airlines is peeled. He will turn that very efficient national airline into an airline of box lunches. I remember from a conversation with him some years ago that the cost of proper service and the better treatment of passengers according to the standard that was being set by a competing airline was causing him to scratch his head in terms of the P&L. He questioned if he could get into this box lunch approach instead of the fancy service which is provided on the airlines. I agree with that in some respects but it is competition that causes good standard of service to be delivered.
My plea to the Minister is that he recognize this serious situation. While I have his attention let me say that I do not know how a company like Canadair with the problems it has can advertise in this manner. 1 do not know how they can do it or what purpose it serves.
While I am on the subject of Canadair, I remember back in 1979-1980 when the problem of the quality of the order book to justify the original investment was brought to my attention. This comes back to the problem of behaviour in that subgovernment and the need for accountability. At that time an order for 25 Challengers was laid on my desk. The person who gave that order in Europe did not have the wherewithal, the means or the intention to buy 25 aircraft. Yet those bookings were the justification for the Government's investment in the first place.
I would like to see Members of Parliament become far more knowledgeable and supported by sound research abilities in our accountability committees. I believe Members should have some expertise to enable them to examine the parameters of and justification for some of these investments. No matter which Government is in power it will be presented with Cabinet documents providing options on which decisions will have to be made. However, I believe that it is ultimately up to us as the elected directors of the shareholders of Canada to do a better job in that respect than is being done presently.
The issue surrounding the water bomber question troubles me. The thing I love about Canada and what I suppose has attracted so many people to this country is that one could come here with nothing. One could be born in poverty, and I believe that it is actually an advantage to be raised in this country with very little in the way of material possessions. People with little gain a burning hunger to want more. Therefore people learned to work, educate themselves, save money and take risks. They may get burnt but would come back again. That is what built this country. If there is no balance in the rule book or a measure of accountability and answerability by this Government's subsector, and it is allowed to run wild, I believe that that dream which energizes so many people will be lost.
With respect to the water bombers, is it fair that because there is a threat of a plant closing down in one city of Canada to subsidize a great fleet of equipment? What does that do to all the independent helicopter operators across the country who sit idle all winter with their equipment waiting to service the provincial needs for forest fires, the mining needs, the
exploration needs and other requirements? Each time a factor such as the water bomber proposal is put into the country's economy, what happens to the private sector that is waiting with its investment in a service? I am thinking in particular of a good operation at Pat Bay which has been carrying on business for years re-engining World War II equipment as water bombers. Is it now in or out of that field of endeavour? I would remind the Minister that even Bill Davis is flying a water bomber these days.
With respect to the accountability equation, for the Minister's benefit I am holding a series of reports from 1978 on. A colleague of his, a former President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State of Economic Development, was deeply involved in this package, as were other Members on his side and on this side. They were calling for an improvement in the accountability equation on this subgovernment.
I would appeal through you, Sir, to Members on the Government side to pay a lot of attention to this because I think it threatens our whole system and society. We are delivering power and privilege to a few people who move through this world. There will be examples coming down very soon of privileges being abused. We are incapable in this House of holding that whole subgovernment sector to account. There has been report after report from the Standing Committee on Public Accounts on this issue, which issue is not being heard by the Liberal Government. It is my plea through this very reasonable Minister of Transport, who has had many bouquets lavished on him today, to carry this concern through because it is very serious. I would like to see us strengthen our function and the delivery of our duties and responsibilities by picking up the challenge that we are dealing with in this motion today.
In closing, if my mother were treated by my late father's employer in the way the Member from Regina's mother was treated when his father died, I would be fighting louder and harder in the socialist camp than I do on this. There is a message for the private sector and for the government sector.
I disagree very much with the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) when he cries out for special privilege for employees employed in Crown corporations and government structures. What about the majority of people employed in the marketplace where the filters of competition, use of capital and accountability apply? I do not think people working for the Government, for CNR, or for Air Canada should enjoy a special privilege. If we are going to talk about equality and equity, let us make available the same privileges in pensions and benefits and everything else more widely across the land. Let us remove this special privilege from those who work our corporate schemes.
Could you let me know how much time I have left, Sir? I see you are indicating that my time has expired. I thank you for your tolerance, Mr. Speaker.

Hear, hear!
June 3, 1983

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am, of course, willing to extend an extra few seconds if the Hon. Member wishes to complete his remarks. He may be satisfied with the opportunity for questions and answers.
Are there any questions and comments?

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). I know he has many valuable ideas regarding accountability. Some of his ideas I would personally like to see implemented in this institution of Parliament.
The Hon. Member for Capilano talks a lot about subgovernment. There is no doubt there is a subgovernment that is becoming more and more powerful while the elected representatives of the people become less and less powerful. There is also in our system what I would now call the fetish of ministerial responsibiitv where Ministers are held accountable for everything within a vast array of departmental networks and Crown corporations. We all know there is no human being who can follow all of those activities and really be accountable for them.
Would the Hon. Member care to comment on the possibility of exchanging the theory and practice of ministerial responsibility for the greater accountability of this subgovernment, as he calls it quite rightly, to committees of Parliament?

Mr. Speaker, that is a very astute question raised by the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport. It is humanly impossible for a Minister to be responsible for the activities within Crown corporations and agencies over and above the activities within his own department. How are you going to judge and evaluate the service of the activities to the objectives as stated? Who will help us with that evaluation?
I think the concept of mininsterial responsibility has to remain, but we also have to move to the concept of deputy minister responsibility in terms of management and in terms of holding the management of departments and corporations accountable for the manner and the efficiency with which they serve, the mandate and the objectives for which they were incorporated to serve. That is where we, as Members of Parliament, fall down in my opinion. That is why I think the accountability equation or system that we in the House have to use has to be separated into two concepts-policy and ministerial responsibility, and management and deputy minister responsibility. I hope there is some move toward a comprehension and an agreement in that area.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member's idea coincides pretty closely with my own with respect to ministerial responsibility. The Minister should be responsible for policy decisions but the administrative responsibility should be assumed and charged to the administrators.
In recent days and for some time we have heard many arguments that the Auditor General should have more access to the books of Crown corporations. I would like the Hon. Member's reaction to that. I have a great concern. If all of
Supply
these Crown corporations are audited by the Auditor General, it seems to me we are creating another of these bureaucratic empires and I wonder in the final analysis who will audit the Auditor General.
I wonder whether the accountability about which the Hon. Member talked in his speech of these Crown corporations to well staffed committees of Parliament would not be a much better route to go. I ask that question because every time we create a stronger central agency it seems to me we slow down the decision-making process.

Mr. Speaker, I would think the Auditor General of Canada by mandate and by Act passed in this House should be the auditor of any Crown corporation or agency requiring a draw on the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada. If it is a Crown corporation that is earning its own way, behaving properly and paying a dividend to its shareholders-the people of Canada-that Crown corporation could go to the private sector. I certainly think the Auditor General of Canada who is an officer of the House-he is the one Officer we have-should have access to the working papers of all audits on Crown corporations and non-departmental agencies.
I think we, as Members in this House, should have access to that kind of information. The Auditor General has to be judicious in how this information is fed to the committees.
The other point made by the Hon. Member was that the standing committees of the House and the four new key accountability committees should be well staffed with research people in order to give us the ability to match that of the bureaucracy around us. I think we are lacking in that area and if we are going to improve the accountability and the answerability equation, we need a higher standard of talent serving us and our needs.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in listening to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), as I always am. I am intrigued by his feeling of outrage that many of us feel and which I think most Members of Parliament feel when we think the taxpayers' interests are not being well represented by agencies of the Crown, such as Crown corporations. I would like to say at this point that I think it is terribly outrageous. I know the Hon. Member's committee, the committee we share, the Public Accounts Committee, on which I cannot participate as much as I would like, but the committee of which I am chairman, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, is looking very carefully and will be over the next couple of weeks at the question of Canadair. It is outrageous that every taxpayer in the country is being asked to invest up to $200 in a corporation which has not yet been able to show that it is a commercially viable operation. I think it is outrageous and I think we should look very carefully at it. I am sure over the next three weeks that we will.
It seems to me that there is another anomaly with regard to Crown corporations which we have to consider carefully. I am

Supply
referring to the fact that the management of Crown corporations does not suffer the same financial loss when the corporations are not profitable as the management of private corporations. Crown corporations can run a perpetual loss. For example, take the case of Canadair. Management salaries not only remained at high levels but continued to increase at a time when the corporation was losing literally hundreds of millions of taxpayers' dollars. I find that offensive and unacceptable. I would like to ask the Hon. Member whether he agrees with that position.

Mr. Speaker, I agree totally with the Hon. Member. The only way as Members of Parliament we can do something about the outrage many of us feel is through improved accountability committees and by arming those committees with good research staff to allow us to dig in and open up, through a good process of disclosure, the many inequities and abuses which are partly human nature but also have no checks and balances. I plead with everyone in the House to start delivering some responsibility back to those people who elected us.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief question for the Hon. Member. What would he think about the suggestion that the Auditor General be the chief adviser to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, or whatever audit committee the House might have, if that committee gained the authority and the staff necessary to go into the details of the audits of various Crown corporations and departments?

I would not be in favour of the Auditor General being the chief adviser to a parliamentary committee. He is a parliamentary officer with a huge mandate to perform. I think the committee would need a strengthened research centre with a very able research director who could call on the office of the Auditor General to provide areas of expertise needed for the wide variety of subject matter with which it would deal.
I think the office and staff of the Auditor General should be available to other committees for specialized problems, in addition to those committees being able to hire specialized expertise for special problems. I would not be in favour of the Auditor General being the chief adviser. He has to be held to account as well.

I know he has been talking about the Auditor General's role and his accountability, but I am concerned, for example, about CN and its operations. If it intends to consolidate services, which could mean the consolidation of personnel and perhaps even the laying off of personnel, how much authority in the Hon. Member's mind should be exerted by Parliament in such a case? Or should we have any authority at all in that area?

The accountability equation has to be dealt with in a non-political or an apolitical environment, and then we marry the two.
