speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had Hon. Members from both the Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party excusing themselves this afternoon because they had planes to catch. They stood up in the House to criticize Crown corporations, but I wonder which mode of transportation they are
June 3, 1983

using to return home today. Yes, they will be using Air Canada and will probably praise its efficiency.
First I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) for using Standing Order 62(11) to bring this topic before the House of Commons. It has allowed all three Parties to put forward their views. 1 always considered the Hon. Member to be a very fair Member of the House. I found him very fair in committee and in the Chamber, but 1 am sorry 1 cannot say that with respect to his motion.
Looking at the motion one would think the whole country is falling apart. He has lost points with me there. To save time I want to point out that there is a lot of control over Crown corporations; if anything, perhaps too much control. There is accountability and there is leadership. The Transport portfolio encompasses some 22 Crown corporations. They fall broadly into the two categories about which we talked this afternoon. The first category is commercial Crown corporations, such as CN, Air Canada, NTCL and Pilotage Authorities. The second category is comprised of commercially oriented Crown corporations which are dependent upon appropriations, such as VIA, Ports Canada and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority.
Despite a great deal of publicity surrounding Crown corporations in general and criticisms thereof by the Auditor General and others, by and large Transport Crown corporations work very well. I believe it is very fair to say that all Crown corporations serve the country well and that steps are constantly being taken by both the corporations and the Government to improve the operation of corporations, their structure and levels of service, to the over-all benefit of Canadians and at reasonable cost to taxpayers where appropriations are required.
The Government for its part has undertaken to improve the situation for both major Canadian railways, and in so doing for the shippers of a wide range of commodities, by proposing revisions to the Crow rate, which I will not get into now.
The Government has recently undertaken to streamline the operations of major ports by introducing a restructured ports organization under the Canada Post Corporation. One of my tasks when I was appointed Parliamentary Secretary was to monitor the Canada Ports Corporation Bill through committee and through the House. The Government introduced Bill C-153, formerly Bill C-123, to further enhance the efficiency of its approval powers for Crown corporation ventures and to enhance the accountability mechanisms available under the many constituent Acts of the corporations.
The corporations themselves are continually updating their managements and organizations to meet the demands of the time. Both CN and Air Canada experienced losses in 1982, as did many private corporations, and both CN and Air Canada have been undertaking adjustments which are intended to reflect today's realities and place them back in a profitable position. These adjustments have often had to be made despite severe opposition in the communities affected, and in some instances losses continue to be absorbed by the corporations as a social responsibility.
Supply
CN, for example, is rationalizing its money-losing express operations and consolidating its complimentary trucking operations. At the same time it continues to operate services for which it loses money, such as Terra Transport, as a social obligation. Air Canada is trimming its over-all capacity and has recently streamlined and pared its management organization. It continues to look for sources of cash such as sales or leases of aircraft currently surplus to its needs. It has recently received approval to reduce its shareholding in a subsidiary corporation at considerable profit.
At the same time Air Canada is also looking at ways in which its long-term cash flow can be improved. This sometimes requires upfront capital expenditures such as investment in a new headquarters building in Montreal which, though some claim to the contrary, represents the best deal for the company in both the short and long-term, and advancing of other expenditures such as the refurbishing of cargo aircraft to meet 1985 Canadian and American noise standards in 1984 instead of 1985.
Northern Transportation Company Limited continues to provide an excellent, reliable, safe and efficient service along the Mackenzie River system, in the Beaufort Sea and on the west coast of Hudson Bay and continues to make a profit. In 1983 it is also absorbing substantial losses at the request of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to continue to provide service at the Athabasca system.
The other Transport corporations continue to function well and largely without controversy, including the Ports Corporation and its 15 ports, the nine Harbour Commissions, the Seaway Authority, the Pilotage Authorities and the bridges.
The motion deals with the Government's loss of control over Crown corporations. Let me demonstrate, Mr. Speaker, that there is already a wide range of control mechanisms in place through general and specific statutes in force. Of overriding importance to all transportation companies, including Crown corporations, are general Acts such as the National Transportation Act, the Aeronautics Act, the Railway Act and the Canada Business Corporations Act. Still of the general nature but with application to Crown corporations alone rather than to all enterprises is the Financial Administration Act.
Finally, many Crown corporations are the creators of their own constituent Acts; examples within Transport Canada are the Air Canada Act, the Canadian National Railways Act, the Canada Ports Corporation Act, the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act. The Financial Administration Act and, where applicable, the constituent Acts and the Canada Business Corporations Act contain many checks on the freedom of Crown corporations to act without prior Government knowledge and approval and many methods through which the activities of Crown corporations can be influenced or controlled by the federal Government.
It would be worth while to examine some of these control mechanisms in more detail in order to illustrate how they do in fact give the federal Government effective control over its

June 3, 1983
Supply
Crown corporations. Perhaps the most basic form of control is through the appointment of the chairman of the board, members of the board of directors and the president and chief executive officer. I was very pleased to hear the compliment paid by the Official Opposition to the Chief Executive Officer of Air Canada. The Air Canada Act and the Canadian National Railways Act specifically reserve these appointments to the Governor in Council. Even in the case of Canada Business Corporations Act Crown corporations, it is the practice of the federal Government to reserve appointments of chairmen and presidents for the Governor in Council. In all cases, Governor in Council appointments of the above nature are for a fixed term with provision made for extension at the Government's discretion. In addition, all such appointees can be removed for cause by the Governor in Council during their term of office. It works both ways.
As a means of exercising practical day to day monitoring of Crown corporation activities, there are frequent unofficial contacts between the Minister of Transport or his senior staff and the President of Air Canada, Canadian National, and other Crown corporations reporting through the Minister of Transport. This serves the Government both as a tool to sense changes in Crown corporation behaviour and financial performance and as an informal means to pass on the wishes of the responsible Minister to the chief executive officer.
The capital budget process is one of the most visible and effective means for the federal Government to control the activities of its Crown corporations. Through the Financial Administration Act, each self-sufficient Crown corporation is obliged to submit a full capital budget for Treasury Board review and Governor in Council approval. Financially dependent Crown corporations are obliged to submit not only a capital budget but also an operating budget. Both Air Canada and Canadian National submit capital budgets for approval through the Minister of Transport.
In submitting capital budgets, Crown corporations must satisfy the federal Government in terms of adequate detail regarding plans and proposed expenditures. The Government can insist on information for subsidiaries as well as for the parent corporation. For example, when Canadian National submitted its 1983 capital budget for approval late in 1982 the company provided, at the Government's request, financial information and planned expenditures broken out for subsidiaries as well as for the parent corporation.
The approval given by the Government to a capital budget is very specific; that is, the Crown corporation has very little latitude in terms of reallocating expenditures and has no authority to exceed the approved expenditure level. If the Crown corporation wishes to do either of these, it must approach the Government with a request for approval of a revised budget. Air Canada has recently done this.
A major control mechanism for the federal Government is the requirement that Crown corporations obtain Government approval before borrowing. Of course, this would include borrowing by the corporation from the Government, but the
Government also has full authority over Crown corporation borrowing from the private sector. The over-all borrowing plans for Crown corporations must be included in the annual capital budget, and are therefore subject to general Government approval. Specific borrowing within the ceilings established in the capital budget is also subject to subsequent approval.
All Crown corporations are required by the Financial Administration Act to submit an annual report which is tabled in Parliament as a public document. Air Canada and Canadian National have consistently met the strict deadlines for submission of annual reports outlined in the Act.
Under their respective Acts, both corporations' annual reports are automatically referred to committee where company officials frequently testify before the estimates as to how the companies have done recently. I would like to compliment all of the members of the Transport Committee for the effective way that they question these officials when they appear before the Transport Committee. I think this is a true sign of parliamentary control and parliamentary accountability.
While the federal Government believes that annual reports provide a good snapshot of corporate performance on an annual basis, it is felt that interim information is also needed to monitor performance adequately. For this reason the Financial Administration Act, Section 75(4), now states that:
A corporation shall make to the appropriate Minister such reports of its financial affairs as he requires.
This very broad authorization gives the Government full power to inquire into the financial affairs of Crown corporations and to take remedial action if required.
In order to ensure the protection of Parliament and the public as the ultimate shareholder of Crown corporations, the federal Government pays close and careful attention to the appointment of auditors. Accounting firms of unimpeachable reputation have been engaged for Air Canada and Canadian National to verify the books of account and records maintained in their support for both companies. The federal Government believes that the reports of these qualified professional auditors are an indispensable tool in monitoring the financial performance of its Crown corporations.
Ministers, their officials and the corporations themselves have been engaged for a year now in intensive study and discussions about the appropriate balance of policies and procedures needed to enable the Government to exercise its responsibilities while ensuring that these corporations are as free as possible to operate in a corporate milieu. Over this period a variety of structures and processes by which the federal Government can give direction to Crown corporations has been developed and modified in response to changing circumstances. In the Air Canada Act, there is a specific and clear provision for direction to the company. Section 8 states that the corporation shall in the exercise of its capacities and the carrying out of its activities, comply with direction of a general nature given to it by order of the Governor in Council.
